subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. Robert D. Nault (Kenora-Rainy River) moves: That this House recognize that the Government's arbitrary and misanthropic policy of unilaterally capping future funding for post-secondary education for Canada's native peoples severely undermines the right and efforts of these peoples to enhance their capacity to make meaningful and lasting improvements to their economic and social conditions and to establish their self-reliance, thereby condemning them to unacceptable living conditions and driving them to desperate measures; and That this House urge the Government to terminate its plans to cap this funding and to take steps to establish effective bilateral consultations on this and other matters vital to the improvement of the lives of and the ending of discrimination toward these Native peoples.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise in the House today in order to debate the issue of native post-secondary education assistance. What does not please me is having to debate this issue at all. The Government's lack of sensitivity to Canada's First Nations people and its lack of understanding of the issues facing them are appalling.
Under a former Liberal Government, funds were committed to the Assembly of First Nations to allow this organization to conduct an intense and thorough review of education for native peoples. This Government lived up to the former Liberal Government's commitment by channelling the necessary funds for this review. This review was recently completed at a cost of $6 million.
What I fail to comprehend in all of this is that the Government, so apparently concerned with spending, has not given this review any consideration whatsoever. The Minister's officials initiated their own review of the
E-12 guidelines, knowing full well that AFN was conducting a similar review. Does the Government not trust the native people of Canada to come up with a policy which would be of benefit not only to the native people but also of benefit to the Government?
It is obvious to all members of my Party that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) has been sandbagged by officials in his own Department. A 1972 policy adopted by a Liberal Government advocated Indian control of Indian education which would see Indian communities taking over the responsibility of education. This policy was developed after the 1971 subcommittee on Indian education heard from the National Indian Brotherhood, now known as the Assembly of First Nations. The NIB had prepared a policy paper which laid the groundwork for federal acceptance of the 1972 policy. This is what consultation does. A Government demonstrates leadership by consulting with the people most affected by a given policy.
Many Hon. Members will no doubt recall the Penner report on Indian self-government which was tabled in this House in November 1983. I need not remind Hon. Members that this report was unanimously endorsed by all three Parties. The Penner report identified education as a critical area of concern. Witnesses appearing before the subcommittee on Indian self-government stated time and time again that First Nations must have control of legislation and policy in order to ensure the survival and development of Indian communities.
In the closing chapter of the Penner report, it states: The Committee is strongly convinced that a major change in the orientation of federal policy must occur. The federal Government must establish new relationships that will enable Indian peoples to break out of the vicious circle of dependency, poverty and despair that now grips them.
This statement is a strong one. It is obviously not a statement the Government understands. If the Government really understood the meaning of establishing new relationships, it would have taken the time to properly consult with First Nations on changes to the E-12 guidelines. This Government could have avoided the backlash against this new policy for native post-secondary education. Had the Government taken the time to negotiate on a bilateral basis, many students would not be risking their lives today by fasting.

April 21, 1989
Supply
Both opposition Parties in the House have raised this issue no fewer than 15 times in the last 14 days of sitting. The Minister claims to have listened to the native peoples of Canada on this issue. If the Minister had really listened to the Indian people, this debate would have been totally unnecessary.
The Government fails to understand that post-secondary education for our native peoples is the key to self-determination and economic self-reliance. Yet the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and members of his Cabinet have repeatedly stated that the country's future is dependent upon economic development. This seems to be a contradiction in terms. Does the Government have one opinion for non-native people and a different one for native people?
The policy is not only restrictive, but it is regressive. By capping the funding for native post-secondary education assistance at $130 million, the policy will restrict the number of native students enrolling in post-secondary institutions. This policy is regressive because it has undone everything which has been achieved by our First Nations in the area of education since 1971.
The changes in this policy will restrict the development of Canada's First Nations and condemn many of them to continuing dependency on the Government from birth until death. Under this Government, Canada's First Nations peoples will not achieve self-determination, nor will they achieve economic self-reliance. This Government has in essence put an end to the hopes and aspirations of many young native people.
I represent 46 native communities in my riding. Many of them have very active and successful economic development projects in the works which will ensure economic self-reliance in the years to come. Jobs have been created for their people. Welfare payments have decreased and so has drug and alcohol abuse. These results have largely been achieved by people who have been through the post-secondary education system and who have returned to their communities with the skills and the knowledge to carry out these policies.
It is no secret that the unemployment rate in our Indian communities runs anywhere from 80 per cent to 95 per cent. It is also no secret that many of our Indian peoples do have not have the minimum number of weeks required to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. The proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act will make matters even worse for our First Nations' peoples. As a result, many of them are on welfare. Last year some $316 million was spent by this Government on welfare pay-outs to Indian people. The changes to the native post-secondary education funding combined with changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act will result in welfare pay-outs of more than $400 million in the next year.
If this Government was committed to deficit reduction, it would lift the cap on native post-secondary education funding. It would not restrict the number of native students enrolling in post-secondary institutions, and it would soon see a dramatic decrease in welfare pay-outs to the Indian people.
The success stories of the native post-secondary education assistance program are many. Nine out of ten native students graduating from post-secondary institutions are employed. For Hon. Members on the opposite side who fail to understand economics, this means that 90 per cent of them have jobs. I remember clearly the words of the Prime Minister during the 1984 election campaign: "Jobs, jobs, jobs". Surely the Prime Minister and his colleagues can understand this.
Indian and Inuit lawyers, doctors, nurses, teachers, and administrators, to name a few, have successfully completed their studies, thanks to a post-secondary education. Those who have chosen not to return to their communities now pay taxes to the Government. I am certain that the Prime Minister and his colleagues understand this.
Canada's native peoples want to make a contribution to society. They do not want Government hand-outs, and they certainly do not want to be dependent upon the Government from birth until death.
April 21, 1989

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I have been listening very carefully to what the Indian peoples have been saying on this issue. The Minister has not been listening, contrary to his very own popular belief. Yes, the Minister has met with the First Nations leaders, and yes, he has stated that he is committed to a bilateral process and the Minister has stated that he will listen. However, I do not believe the Hon. Minister understands what is at stake. If the Minister and his officials had only undertaken a full bilateral consultation from the very beginning, we would not be here today debating this very critical issue.
Once again the Minister will tell us that he has consulted with the Indian people. I have yet to come across a single individual from the native community who supports the restrictive and regressive changes to native post-secondary education funding. Not one.
In fact, I have received well over 1,500 individual petitions from native communities, and more than 100 letters from various native groups and associations, all of which are in my riding. I will bet that the Minister's office has been bombarded with letters and petitions opposing the changes to native post-secondary education assistance. How can the Minister and this Government state that they have consulted with the Indian peoples?
The priorities of this Government are misplaced. Let us compare what it costs to put a young native student through college or university with what it costs to support that same native student on welfare. At today's rates a young native student can get a good, solid education for approximately $35,000. Once that young native student graduates, he or she finds a job and is self-supporting.
Now let us look at what it would cost the Government to support that same native student by way of welfare. If the Government had to support the student by way of welfare for the rest of his or her life, and providing that the individual remained unmarried, it could cost the taxpayers close to $300,000. Imagine what the costs would be if that same individual were to marry and have three or four children. Where is the logic?
When it comes to paying the costs for holding native youth in jail, there is no shortage of government money. There is no shortage of government money either when it comes to paying a lifetime of welfare and poverty.
Supply
This Government has under-estimated the strength of Canada's aboriginal peoples. We have seen demonstrations at Indian Affairs offices across the country, resulting in the arrests of several native people. We have also seen protests by our First Nations here on Parliament Hill, and we have seen hunger strikes by native students frustrated by this Government's new policy. The First Nations will continue to oppose the policy of the Government with respect to native post-secondary education. The opposition Parties will continue to oppose this policy. The Government will not be let off the hook until the Minister of Indian Affairs agrees to some serious bilateral negotiations, without deadlines and restrictions, with the native leadership.
The Minister of Indian Affairs will not lose face by admitting that he has made a mistake. In fact, if the Minister will only compromise on the question of bilateral negotiations without deadlines, he will be respected and admired for his commitment to the Indian people of Canada. I am afraid that if the Minister does not move quickly on this issue, he will lose all credibility with the people for whom he is responsible. If that happens, the Prime Minister will have no other choice but to remove him from his duties.
Support for the First Nations' views on native post-secondary education is growing. Many non-native Canadians have had an opportunity to truly look at both sides of this issue and have come to understand and support First Nations in their fight against these restrictive and regressive changes.
The native leadership and students have received support from the Canadian Federation of Students, from university professors, from teachers, from labour organizations, from churches, from social justice coalitions, and from our very own Human Rights Commissioner. How can the Government continue to ignore the importance of this issue? How can this Government implement changes to a policy without proper consultation? It is time for the Government to live up to its commitment of a bilateral negotiation process with the native leadership and the students. It is time for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to make peace with the native peoples and negotiate in good faith without time limits.
I sincerely hope that the Government, and in particular the Minister who is here today, will have paid close attention to what I have said and I hope that it will pay close attention to what Hon. Members speaking after me will say.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by expressing my appreciation to the Minister who has agreed to switch the order in speaking today. I think this could be mutually beneficial. I welcome the opportunity to speak now in part because I wanted the Minister to have the opportunity to reply to matters just raised by the person who led off this debate for the Liberal Party and by myself.
Having said that, I want to stress that in my judgment we are having this debate today in the House of Commons not primarily because people on the Opposition side of the House or people on the Government side of the House in some abstract way decided as a matter of equity that we ought to be debating the condition of the aboriginal community in Canada, but more specifically because of the condition of education at the post-secondary level in which aboriginal Canadians are involved. The reason we are having this debate, and it is crucial for us in Parliament to understand this, is that 31 days ago some young aboriginal Canadians decided to embark upon a kind of protest that regrettably, in terms of human reality in this country, they knew would be necessary to provoke the Parliament of Canada into having a serious debate on their condition. I am convinced we are having the debate because some young Canadians of aboriginal ancestry in Thunder Bay decided, to put it bluntly, to raise a little hell. I am convinced that is why we are having the debate.
The reason is that they perceived that in a policy, initiated some two years ago and finalized in one sense in March of this year, the Government has as its ultimate objective, if it were carried through, not to increase opportunities for young aboriginal Canadians but to curtail opportunities that have been growing in recent years. In short, this policy which ought to be aimed at

greater equality is going to lead to more inequality. Young aboriginal Canadians were right in initiating a protest. We are right in having this debate today. I hope the Government will do the right thing by reversing its policy.

As I have already indicated, when you look at what started 31 days ago, a lot of Canadians could be excused for thinking it was a protest about some obscure Government regulation or set of regulations, labelled E-12 guidelines, emanating from one part of the federal bureaucracy. As we know, that is not the case. The details involved in this issue are important. The particulars involved in the dispute about post-secondary education are important.
What is fundamentally involved in this issue, as aboriginal Canadians first and foremost understand, and as parts of the trade union community, the university community, and Members of Parliament are finally understanding in this debate, is whether we are going to perpetuate inequality in Canada as it affects aboriginal Canadians, or whether we are going to move forward to a greater degree of equality. That is what is at stake in this debate.
I would like to put it in that kind of perspective. We as a nation outside the aboriginal community take pride in our democratic institutions. We teach our children that whether it is the Parliament of Canada, our judicial system, our federal system, or our range of liberties, our freedom to be what we want to be, this is a good and just country. It has its imperfections that all of us, certainly on this side of the House, are constantly preoccupied in trying to remove one by one. The basic structure of the common reality that most of us share is one that makes us the envy of a good part of the people on this planet.
If most of us can look with pride at what has been achieved, and point to particular instances that are a source of that pride, can any Canadian seriously point with pride to the aboriginal reality of Canada? I know that one of the most moving documents to have emerged, in its plain, sparse and lucid language, certainly in my lifetime as a politician, describes that reality. I am speaking about sections of the report of the Human Rights Commissioner, whose report came down just some two weeks ago, implemented. This is a document that should become required reading in every school across Canada.
Last week the Human Rights Commissioner issued in part his assessment of the human rights aspect of the existence of aboriginal Canadians. Without exception, we see this as some kind of report card. In the large majority of aspects of human existence, according to the assessment of the Human Rights Commissioner of Canada, the existence of our aboriginal peoples has to be seen as one of profound injustice. It is an existence that none of us, on either side of the House or outside the House as Canadians, should be viewing with pride or with anything less than an attitude that says something has to be done and done quickly to remedy the injustices.
He said the following: "The grand promise of equality of opportunity stands in stark contrast to the conditions in which many native people live". He went through them item by item and aspect by aspect of human life. For example, an Indian girl bom in 1980 can expect to live nearly seven years less than her non-native schoolyard girlfriend. Unemployment, the exception for most Canadians, is the norm for aboriginal Canadians. Imagine someone in Toronto or Winnipeg, in a non-aboriginal family, growing up and expecting an unemployment rate in those cities of 60 to 90 per cent? If that were the situation in any of our urban communities, there would be a revolution. That is the reality for aboriginal Canadians.
Apart from labour and the right to get a job, what about income? If an Indian is lucky enough to find work on a reserve, he or she can expect to earn barely in excess of half of the average income of the general population, some 54 per cent. Off the reserve, as the Human Rights Commissioner has pointed out, aboriginal Canadians are under-represented in terms of their percentage of the population in virtually every sector of the Canadian economy in the workplace. Is it any wonder that so many aboriginal Canadians live on welfare, and that so many end up in prison? It happens to be the case that 55 per cent of the on reserve population will receive some form of social assistance.
As the Human Rights Commissioner has pointed out, it is the case that "an Indian youngster in Canada has a better chance of being sent to prison than of completing university". I would be surprised if that were said of a part of a population in any other part of the world. I remind all Members of the House that these are aboriginal peoples. There is a certain historical myth about two founding races in this country. When it was developed it was said to be that the English and the French were the founding races. That in itself is illustrative of racism. The founding people of this country are the aboriginal peoples, and they are the people who have been most unjustly treated. If you look at the reality described in
April 21, 1989

these statistics about opportunities to work, income, who is in our prisons and who is collecting welfare, the picture is unbelievably bad as it affects our aboriginal community. There is one exception to that. It is the one we are talking about today, that is, the educational opportunities available, and available just recently, to young aboriginal Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, in 1960, only 60 natives were registered in Canadian universities and only 3.4 per cent of native students finished high school. At that time, native youths were taken from their homes and sent to boarding schools in faraway communities. These children had to adjust to a new school environment in a strange language and culture. Children had to learn under such conditions.
Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising that this approach was a failure. The Government finally began to do what we now take for granted. It built schools in native communities. It put an end to the practice of punishing young native children when they spoke their mother tongue in class.
Today, we finally see young native university-trained teachers return to the village of their birth and teach the rising generation. And it works, Mr. Speaker!
The new generation of native teachers now takes part in curriculum development and language studies and they are models for their students.
Today, ten times as many students finish high school as in 1960.

From 1960 until two years ago the federal Government offered post-secondary assistance to any aboriginal student who met the entrance requirements. There was real progress during this period. In short, the program, to use the language of the city, was open-ended. It was designed to meet all the needs demonstrated by the aboriginal community. If there was a desire to go on to further education, then at long last during this period the federal Government said that the federal Treasury would ensure that money would be available for students' access to that education. As long as there was a need, the commitment was to ensure that that need would be met.
Supply
This program has its flaws, as was pointed out to the Government by members of the aboriginal community as well as by those outside who were doing an assessment of it. However, the crucial point I want to make is that the program was working. As a result of it, there are today some 15,000 aboriginal students in universities and colleges across Canada. The number is increasing every year.
Having said that, it is also important to know that even these numbers represent a participation rate at the post-secondary and university level of 4 per cent of the native population compared with 27 per cent for the national average. The program was a start in the right direction. Aboriginal people were prepared to accept it and prepared to build on it.
However, two years ago the program was working so well the Government decided to fix it. At a time when aboriginal people were finally starting to use the program, the Government decided to limit financial accessibility. The Department of Indian Affairs introduced a fixed annual budget and introduced a ranking system that discouraged enrolment flexibility. The latest round of changes which were announced in March of this year and which took effect in April saw a capping of the program. Aboriginal people, students and adults alike, feared that this was a major step in the wrong direction. They were right. We are going to do everything we can to get the Government to reverse itself.

That is the point. If the Minister is prepared to get to his feet today and say what he said in that letter is no longer Government policy, that all the funds that are necessary without qualification are going to be made available, then we will support him in that change and say so publicly.
It is precisely to this kind of letter written last month-not last year-by the Minister that the young students and the aboriginal community have been reacting. Canadians with a sense of decency and commitment to equality have been reacting to it as well.
What the Government was doing and saying in justification of the program was that it hopes to save money. The Government has been using some figures. Well, I have some figures as well.
It costs an average of $7,200 to pay for one year of post-secondary education for a native student. It costs $14,000 to cover the cost of training a young man or woman to become a nurse or, in short, to become a self-supporting contributor to the whole of the community instead of being dependent upon it for the rest of his or her life. Surely there is a moral and economic improvement involved in this that constitutes an immense improvement over life of petty crime and welfare dependency. I say to the Government so preoccupied with cost-cutting, a Government that seems to be run by accountants instead of human beings concerned with improving human welfare, that surely it makes more sense to provide money for education than it does to build prisons. Surely it makes more sense to educate aboriginal Canadians than to keep them dependent upon welfare. Surely it makes more sense to treat an aboriginal Canadian as having the same right to human dignity that comes from self-fulfilment as a white person in our society. As soon as we understand that, we will make sure that the money is available.

First, we believe that there should not be a cap where there is a legitimate need for aboriginal Canadians for education. We believe it is long overdue. The rest of us pay for that. They have paid for it indirectly themselves as ultimate contributors to Canadian society. However, we believe that we have an obligation in the Parliament of Canada to make sure that money is available for that.
Second, in terms of the process itself, we believe that the desire of the students initially supported by aboriginal leaders for the Minister to suspend implementation of this program for the coming academic year makes sense. Keep the old regulations in place for the coming year. Work out with the aboriginal community during the coming months a new set of regulations or proposals that are acceptable both to the aboriginal community and to the Government of Canada. Surely that makes sense.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I conclude now with this point. A former Member of Parliament, Jim Manly, who was for many years the critic for my Party on Indian Affairs, once used what I think is a wonderful metaphor for the rest of us to consider. It was a metaphor involving a canary. Jim used to put it something like this. He said that when miners went into the mines they took a canary with them. They used to look at the canary and observe it. As the canary began to weaken they knew it would not be long before they would begin to weaken; that if the canary died then they would die. I would like to extend Jim Manly's metaphor in this way.
We should begin to see aboriginal Canadians as our canary. Whenever they suffer, we are going to suffer. Whenever they experience inequality, we experience inequality. The real objective ought not to be to contain the canary. The real objective ought to be to set the canary free. The real means of achieving that for aboriginal Canadians is for them, as they have been doing, to produce their own generation of leaders. The programs that have been put in place have been producing not hundreds, but thousands of new, self-possessed, competent, committed leaders in the aboriginal community. We should do everything we can to further that process, not inhibit it. We should not take steps that would lead to the suffocation of this canary, but to its liberation. When it is liberated and not until then will the rest of us will not be able to regard ourselves as a truly free people.



April 21, 1989

I visit and talk with them quite often.
Did not the Hon. Member for Oshawa this morning in his statement give some false impressions or try to capitalize on the plight of some natives? He indicated his Party is perceived now to be the only one concerned about native Canadians. As a matter of fact during the Thirty-Third Parliament, his Party never once put forth an emergency debate in this House with regard to natives. Yet today he wants to be the champion of natives.
Let me ask him some questions in view of his statements. How can the Hon. Member say that the budget has been capped when in fact the increase has been 10 per cent per year? That is a fact he forgot to mention this morning.

How can he stand and tell Canadians we have cut their budgets? In fact, we have not. I would like some answers, and so would Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to that particular well-informed question. I would like to respond. I first of all never said that we were the only people concerned. In fact, I went out of my way to say that there was a policy that was started in 1960. We were not the Government then. I gave the Government at that time credit, some Members here were Ministers of the Crown in that Government. I am prepared to do that. I have as recently as yesterday paid public tribute to the Minister involved in the issue as a man who has shown humane concern, not only in his present portfolio, but in his previous one. What the Member says about that is just totally wrong.
Supply
I have referred to the issue of capping. Indeed, I used that language. In reports I have had and in discussion with the Minister, as well as the document I put on the record that the Minister wrote-at least he signed it, he is responsible for it-it said: "They want a budget that could not continue to grow at the pace of the last decade". The Minister will comment on it. According to the students, and I have not seen him deny this publicly, he has refused unequivocally to say that there will be a total open-ended budget. Whatever the need, it should be met, not in terms of moving people from the back of the line to the front of the line, but from the point of view of removing the line. That is our policy.
What we now have with the present Government is not 10, 12, 20, 30 or 40, but hundreds of students who cannot get into post-secondary education because funds have not been available. That is the reality. The funds have been there have been inadequate. We are saying, meet the need, provide the funds, have an open-ended budget. As long as there is need for education, make sure the money is available. That is my reply to the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, VIA Rail is a hot topic in the news these days. As usual, VIA being in the news is not necessarily good news for the people of northern Manitoba.
After the NTA hearings, the public relations people cited the Winnipeg-Churchill run as follows: "Apart from providing a social service, it is hard to justify that route". The Ottawa Citizen, upon receiving that information said that the Winnipeg-Churchill run is a horror story. Other papers, taking VIA's PR lead, have agreed.

April 21, 1989
5. ft 31
I think it is important that the truth be told. For many people in northern Ontario, VIA Rail is still the only available form of transportation to other communities. It is in effect the lifeline to the North. VIA takes people to their grocery shopping. It takes people to the doctor. VIA takes people to their friends and family.
For years we in the North have watched in anger as stations have been closed down and the frequency of trains has been cut back. Train fares, of course, have continued to rise.

VIA has said the train is not being used. It had better provide the service, then it will have the usage. If the Government's slogan is "use it or lose it", make it usable.

Mr. Speaker, once again the Government is scaring the people of Atlantic Canada with more rumours of cut-backs. This time it is attacking the Atlantic transportation industry by removing two vital subsidies, the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act.
We know that transportation is the cornerstone of regional economic development and these programs have been just that in Atlantic Canada for over 60 years.

STUDENT LOAN REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that post-secondary education in Canada is becoming a matter of increasing public concern, it was with considerable dismay that I read in The Canada Gazette of March 18 that the Government is proposing an amendment to the Canada student loans regulations which will reduce amounts available to students and set lifetime limits on student loan borrowing.
Young Canadians in the gallery take note. This lifetime cap of $20,000 for undergraduates is less than 50 per cent of the maximum amount currently available.
There are several problems here. One is that the caps are too low.
A sum of $5,000 per year will not allow a student to attend university full-time, especially since many students are not able to find employment to supplement this amount.
Another is that family income tables have not been adjusted for several years. This impacts negatively on a student's capacity to obtain student loans.
Third, this proposed program is not only inflexible but is totally at odds with the Government's stated concerns for retraining. The lifetime cap will effectively prevent people from returning to university.
This appears to be another ploy to force the provinces to increase their provincial bursary programs and allow the Government to shirk further its responsibility to the youth of the nation. I ask the Minister responsible to give this matter his immediate attention so that students can plan for the upcoming year.

In view of the statements made that no change will be made, can the Deputy Prime Minister reassure the House that the Minister of Finance will be instructed that no changes will be made to the federal government contribution to unemployment insurance funds?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subtopic: FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will repeat all the benefits Newfoundland will enjoy as a result of the unemployment insurance reform announced last week: access to employment, access to better paying employment and access to training.
As for your main question about what will happen on April 27, I would ask you to be patient and to wait until the Minister of Finance brings down his budget. You will get your answer in a matter of days!

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FUNDING OF CO-OPERATIVE EDUCATION PROGRAM
FUNDING OF CO-OPERATIVE EDUCATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on a very important point raised earlier. My question is directed to the Minister of Youth.
As the youngest Member of Parliament I am deeply offended and, frankly, disillusioned by the announcement made yesterday by the Minister that the Government intends to steal money from the unemployed to pay for co-op education for young people.

April 21, 1989
Oral Questions
How does the Minister justify breaking a sacred campaign promise made by the Prime Minister that the Unemployment Insurance Program would not be changed?
How can the Minister pit two needy groups in our society, the young and the unemployed, against each other?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: FUNDING OF CO-OPERATIVE EDUCATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me congratulate the Hon. Member on his election to the House of Commons, and welcome him here. I am sorry that after a few days in the House of Commons he has already declared himself disillusioned. I am also a young Member of Parliament, and I am not disillusioned at all.
The Hon. Member should know, if he is so interested in the issues related to youth, the real issues related to youth are that those in our society who are the most vulnerable are the young people who drop out of high school, and the young people who have the lowest level of education in our society.
After four or five years of Progressive Conservative Government we have the lowest unemployment rate for young people in the last 17 years.
The money used in co-op education will be used under the CJS Fund, and money made available because of the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REQUEST THAT FUNDING BE MADE AVAILABLE FROM GENERAL REVENUES
REQUEST THAT FUNDING BE MADE AVAILABLE FROM GENERAL REVENUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. I would advise the Minister that I also agree with co-op education, but I do not agree with it being done on the backs of unemployed Canadians.
Not only is the Minister breaking a sacred promise made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign, but he is also breaking the promise made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration who stated that the money that she is taking away from the Unemployment Insurance Fund will only go to train unemployed people.
How does the Minister justify breaking this promise? Will the Minister get serious about co-op education and fund the program from general revenues, rather than taking funds from the unemployed people who desperately need them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST THAT FUNDING BE MADE AVAILABLE FROM GENERAL REVENUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me applaud the Hon. Member for actually stating, I presume on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada, that this is the first time they are actually for something, including co-op education. That is something new.
Let me assure the Hon. Member that it is quite clear that the money that will be saved through UI reform will go to people who are unemployed. That initiative will enable the Government to have more flexibility through the Canadian Jobs Strategy which will enable the Government to quadruple the amount of money that will be put into co-op education, which the Hon. Member is for.
May I conclude by asking the Hon. Member to stop fighting change, and stop being a dinosaur. He must accept the fact that we live in a new world where change in inevitable, and this country has to face up to that.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Approximately half an hour ago the Minister of State for Indian Affairs stated there was no cap on the Government's program as it affects post-secondary education for aboriginal Canadians.
Would the Minister comment on the accuracy of that view?
As the Minister knows, a good part of the motivation for the concern of students affected is that there has been a cap.
I refer to the letter of the Minister dated March 20, 1989, in which he stated: "The program will have to live within its annual allocation-". If that is not a cap, what is it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ABORIGINAL PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated on numerous occasions, both inside and outside the House, two years ago my predecessor announced that the program would have to function within budget. This is exactly what the program has been doing for two years. Annually a budget is determined with respect to this particular program.
April 21, 1989

As I have indicated on numerous occasions, if the needs increase, in my humble opinion the funding for the program will increase in order to meet those needs.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on page 1 of the same letter the Minister talks about the need to stop the growth of the budget because it cannot "continue to grow at the pace of the last decade". I have already quoted him as saying that it has to live within its annual allocation. In the same paragraph the Minister states that this will mean that a "number of students will temporarily have to seek those sources of support available to-other Canadians", because there will not be spaces available.
The Minister cannot have it both ways. He has just stated in the House that if there is going to be a need, and the students have that need, presumably they will not have to seek other sources. In the letter the Minister states that they have to seek outside sources. Is the Minister now saying that they will not have to seek outside sources, and that the Government will provide all the money needed for a young aboriginal person who wants to attend post-secondary education? Is that the policy? If so, make it clear, please.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we must also look at the guidelines. The guidelines state that assistance will be provided within the limits of funds voted by Parliament.

subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext: That is a cap.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext:
That is voted annually. That is why each year we will look at the needs and determine what funds we need to meet those needs.
If the Hon. Member also wants to quote from my letter, he should also quote the second to last paragraph which states:
But no program design endures forever. In light of the many constructive responses the Department has received, I am instructing my officials -

subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext: Dispense.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext: Table it.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: MINISTER'S LETTER-BUDGET FOR PROGRAM
speechtext:
Hon. Members opposite do not want to hear the truth.
I am instructing my officials to review the policy periodically to ensure that it keeps pace with the changing needs and aspirations of students in your communities.
Oral Questions
Obviously the increase in the number of students will justify the increase of funds for this particular program. I have been saying that from the outset.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FUNDING REQUIREMENTS OF STUDENTS
FUNDING REQUIREMENTS OF STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reality is that the Minister has not been saying that from the outset.
Without exception the aboriginal Canadians with whom I have spoken, and there are many fair-minded Canadians among them, do not understand the Minister to have the policy he now states. They understand his correspondence to state that there is a cap.
I want to clear this up. Is the Minister saying, unlike what he states in his letter, that any student in the coming academic year of 1989-1990 who wants to go to post-secondary education will receive funding this year from the Government of Canada? Yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: FUNDING REQUIREMENTS OF STUDENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been saying from the start that there is an annual budget and that we will be seeking funds on an annual basis with respect to the demand increases that will come from year to year. That is why there has to be an exchange with the native population, which I have encouraged from the start, which I have instructed my officials to continue in order to ensure that we have the appropriate data to seek the appropriate funds to continue a program in which the Government believes. This program has gone from $4.2 million to $130 million, which is an increase of 30 times.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FINANCE

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Yesterday, the Bank of Canada raised the bank rate to 12.61 per cent. The real interest rate in Canada is now over 8 per cent, the highest level in 20 years. The spread between Canadian and American interest rates is more than 2 per cent, compared with historical spreads of 1 per cent.

April 21, 1989
Oral Questions
Why is the Conservative Government attacking Canadian consumers with this high interest rate policy?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subtopic: FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I don't think Canadians want to go back to the severe recession we experienced under the Liberal Government in the early eighties.
As you know, current interest rates are part of the Bank of Canada's general policy to fight the threat of inflation.
As for the spread between Canadian and American interest rates, let us not forget that while today, the spread for 90-day commercial paper is 2.6 per cent, in the early eighties it was as high as 4 per cent.
We intend to continue to support the Bank of Canada in its efforts to ensure that interest rates will go down in time, and do so permanently, in the best interests of Canadian consumers.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: MORTGAGE AND CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MORTGAGE AND CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext: I come now to the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. All Canadians are affected by the high interest rate policy of this Government. One year ago an $80,000 mortgage was financed at 9.75 per cent.

subtopic: MORTGAGE AND CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Who is talking about high interest rates?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MORTGAGE AND CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Today that same mortgage is renewed at 13 per cent, an additional cost of $2,000 a year.
We also know that on June 1 the interest rate charged on credit cards will rise to more than 20 per cent. Why is the Government maintaining this high interest rate policy which is difficult and disastrous for Canadian families?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subtopic: MORTGAGE AND CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that the Government has been monitoring the economic situation in Canada very carefully. In four years we have shown that we have been able to deal with the situation. However, losing control of the economy and letting interest rates become even more devastating as a result of increased inflation will certainly do nothing to improve the situation to which the Hon. Member is referring.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROTECTION OF CANADIAN RESEARCH COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Andre).
Given the fact that branch plants do not do research, that there is a lack of risk capital for Canadian research companies and that foreigners take over Canadian firms like Lumonics, Connaught Laboratories, what does the government intend to do to protect our research companies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROTECTION OF CANADIAN RESEARCH COMPANIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question begs a speech of at least 40 minutes to go over all of the things this Government is doing to demonstrate our commitment to research and development-the establishment of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, the establishment of NAPS, the $240 million to Centres of Excellence, the $200 million extra to granting agencies, and the $80 million for the Canadian Scholarships Program. There is a whole range of programs to indicate our Government's commitment to science and technology and industrial development in this country.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: ACQUISITION OF COMPANIES BY FOREIGN INTERESTS
ACQUISITION OF COMPANIES BY FOREIGN INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister had the opportunity to give a 40-minute speech yesterday and he did not address the question of Canadian ownership. He has pointed out the problem himself. He is quoted in Computer Dealer News for March 9, 1989 as saying:
If three or four branch plants close, due to free trade and the
economic restructuring we're witnessing, that will, perhaps, facilitate
the creation of one Canadian firm to fill the void, one that will
conduct R and D.
I think this is known as the Khmer Rouge method of developing a research community.
The Minister continued:
Branch plants just don't do research.
Does the Government think that Canadian control of our research companies is important? If so, what is it going to do about these sell-offs?
April 21, 1989

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ACQUISITION OF COMPANIES BY FOREIGN INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Investment Canada Act provides that only those take-overs which are a net benefit to Canada, including research and development, are allowed to proceed. The Act is there.
If the Hon. Member has some evidence of where, in fact, the Act does not provide that, let him bring it forward, but these blanket, wildly unsubstantiated charges are absurd.
I would remind the Hon. Member that it was his Party which fought Bill C-22 to the bitter end, a Bill which has brought about hundreds of millions of dollars of research and development in this country. I am glad to see that the new Member is showing a break from that terrible Liberal tradition of saying one thing and acting in another way.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: INTERROGATION OF SCIENTIST BY MILITARY POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. An Alberta scientist, Dr. Mendoza, whom I had telephoned about atmospheric nerve gas tests in Alberta, was recently taken to a motel room in Medicine Hat and interrogated by military police. He was denied the right to legal counsel at the interrogation.
According to Dr. Mendoza the interrogation focused on my communication with the scientist, a communication that I would point out was never made public.
Why was the scientist denied legal counsel? Is it the view of the Government that communication between Members of Parliament and public servants is somehow improper?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: INTERROGATION OF SCIENTIST BY MILITARY POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the Member, as I am sure he is aware-I think he has had correspondence with Dr. Mendoza for some years in official capacities- that we have within the Department of National Defence a regular review of security clearances. Dr. Mendoza has had those interviews, voluntary interviews, I might advise the Member. Of course, for any further concerns that Dr. Mendoza may have there is an appro-
Oral Questions
priate grievance procedure in the Department through which he may address those grievances.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: BURGLARY OF MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT'S OFFICE
BURGLARY OF MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT'S OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
My office was broken into here on the Hill on March 6 and the confidential files, including my communication with Dr. Mendoza, were gone through. A few days later Dr. Mendoza was interrogated without legal counsel. According to Dr. Mendoza the military police described revelations about Suffield as being politically embarrassing.
Do the military in Canada work for the Conservative Party or for the people of Canada? Don't Albertans have the right to know that the air they breathe is being used for open atmospheric nerve gas tests?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: BURGLARY OF MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT'S OFFICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the allegations made by my colleague are quite serious and I advised him yesterday that I would check upon them with the Commissioner of the RCMP. I discussed the matter at length with him this morning and he has advised me that he has been in touch with the Toronto and Ottawa City police concerning the pattern which according to the Hon. Member does exist in the various break-ins. I have been informed by the Commissioner, and I made a careful examination of the information given to me, that no pattern emerges out of these break-ins, Mr. Speaker, and that the Hon. Member has not asked directly any police force to investigate what happened in his office.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for External Relations. Canadians are concerned about the tragic events that are taking place in Lebanon. There has been a fresh outburst of armed conflict in that country, centred in Beirut. Bombardments affect the civilian population indiscriminately, claiming thousands of victims. Could the Minister inform the House about the measures taken by Canada to offer help to the people of Lebanon, the victims of this terrible war?

April 21, 1989
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his question, which gives me an opportunity to inform the House and all other Canadians about the measures Canada has put in place to help the Lebanese people who are now suffering the consequences of a devastating war. I think that at this point, Mr. Speaker, we should make a distinction between the assistance extended to the Lebanese that remain in their country and the assistance given to those who are trying to escape the combat zones.
At the present time, our embassy in Damascus is able to provide all immigration services. We have four officers on the spot, and I can give the Members of this House and all Canadians the assurance that our services are able to cope with the demand. Yesterday, we heard from our representative in Syria that Lebanese citizens can enter Syria on their Lebanese I.D. Card or passport.
People living in the Christian sector of Beirut, have passports that will get them to Cyprus. As for the services we are able to offer in Cyprus at the present time, I said yesterday in a statement in the House that we had a consular officer on the spot, and I can inform Hon. Members that in Cyprus, it is estimated that since the beginning of March between 11,000 and 15,000 Lebanese have applied to emigrate to various countries. In fact, most have already left Cyprus. As for applications for admission to Canada, all I can say is that we are able to cope with the demand for the time being-

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Order!

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I would like to add that as for the services we are offering people in Lebanon, I announced this week that half a million dollars-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am sorry but I will have to interrupt the Minister. The Hon. Member for Saint-Laurent.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: SITUATION OF THOSE CLAIMING REFUGE STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was meant for the Minister of Employment and
Immigration, but in her absence it is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
We have waited long enough for news about the hearings that are supposed to take place in Montreal and Toronto to deal with the tremendous backlog of refuge claims!
The Minister knows perfectly well that the backlog of refugee claims in our large urban areas is a very real problem. Why the delay in establishing bodies that will decide whether these refugees will be allowed to stay? When does the Government intend to deal with the ever increasing problem of refugees waiting to have their claims heard, both in Montreal and Toronto?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: SITUATION OF THOSE CLAIMING REFUGE STATUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my colleague who is responsible for Immigration, I would like to reassure Canadians and tell them that since we introduced our new refugee status determination process, things have become much easier. The figures prove that the system works well, and I can give Canadians the assurance that although there is still room for improvement, current evaluation reports are very positive.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS
PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. In a press release on March 31 we were informed that the Immigration and Refugee Board is developing new facilities in Montreal and Toronto. What does the Government plan to do to alleviate the refugee backlog in Montreal and Toronto? Why is the Government planning two different systems, one for Montreal and Toronto and one for the rest of Canada? Why does the Government not have a policy that treats all refugee claimants equally?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subtopic: PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have a system in use across the country, in Montreal as well as in Toronto. I repeat, the measures we have put in place during the last few months are working well, and we are satisfied with the results.



April 21, 1989

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS
PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Public Works. On Tuesday, April 19, the Welland Canal Development Board held a press conference at which it released the contents of a report that suggested how the Welland Canal lands could be developed. Even though I am a member of the board I have not yet received a copy of the report, a report which cost $30,000.
Has the Minister been apprised of this report? Does he agree with the recommendations of it, one of which is that the Welland Canal lands be sold to the highest bidder?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question affords me the first opportunity I have had to congratulate my colleague on his re-election to the House.
I wish to inform him that, yes, I have been apprised of the report. I also wish to reassure him that this consultant's report was only intended to identify potential development of the land. I emphasize the word "potential".
I understand his concern that any private development might impinge on the public use of the land. I am pleased to tell him that there will be further consultations. Nothing definitive will be done without input from the City of Welland and, as far as I am concerned, from the Hon. Member himself.

speakerposition: subtopic

REQUEST FOR PUBLIC MEETINGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Minister assure the House and, indeed, the people of my riding, that in future all of the meetings of the board will be held in public so that indeed the public can be apprised of what is going on and how the deliberations are proceeding?

Oral Questions HOUSING

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REQUEST THAT SPECULATORS' TAX BE INTRODUCED
REQUEST THAT SPECULATORS' TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of State for Housing. There have been repeated calls to cool off the hot real estate market in Vancouver and Toronto by imposing a tax on speculative real estate profits. Yet the Minister of Housing keeps saying that he will have to do more with less in terms of solving the critical housing crisis in Canada.
If the Minister is short of funds why is he ignoring the money that could be realized from the imposition of a speculators' tax on real estate property?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
subtopic: REQUEST THAT SPECULATORS' TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I am sure the Hon. Member is aware, I had an opportunity to visit Vancouver last month to see for myself the red-hot real estate market in Vancouver. It is certainly one of the hot spots of housing in the country.
At that time I had the opportunity to meet with the Minister of Housing for the Province of British Columbia, the Mayor of Vancouver, the Mayor of Coquitlam, and other providers of market and social housing in and around the Vancouver area, in an effort to try to come to grips with and to see if there is not a way to solve the problems, and have the federal Government made a part in that process.
One of the suggestions of the Hon. Member has to do with land speculation tax. That is a very interesting possibility.
When I was a Private Member I urged the Province of Ontario to institute such a tax. Perhaps the Hon. Member might like to urge the Province of British Columbia to do the same.
My advice at the moment is that that sort of a tax would have to be imposed by a provincial Government. However, if my advice changes I will certainly advise the Hon. Member.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION
MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is addressed to the same Minister. He is undoubtedly aware that in the last few days a piece of property was sold by the B.C. Government to a numbered company for $2.2 million and resold the same day for $10.5 million.

April 21, 1989
Oral Questions
When the Minister was a back-bencher he advocated that the federal Government introduce a speculation tax. Will the Minister explain why he has changed his mind, and that it is not the federal Government's responsibility but a provincial responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
subtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I explained to the Hon. Member, my current advice now is that such a tax is one that must be levied by the provincial Government. If my advice changes, the Hon. Member will certainly be advised. I share his concern about property flipping over at a great rate at veiy inflated prices.

subtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
subtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: There is an awful lot of excitement from Members opposite, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: All the fire is gone!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
subtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Certainly, part of my discussions with the Province of British Columbia and with other jurisdictions is to try to co-operate to prevent things like that in the future.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: CONTAMINATION OF SOIL AND WATER IN THE ROUYN-NORANDA AND VAL-D'OR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. A recent study tabled some months ago with the Quebec Environment Department and made public by an environmental group in my region this week would show that the ground and streams in the area of Rouyn-Noranda and Val-d'Or are seriously contaminated by heavy metals. So, Mr. Speaker, since this is a serious situation that may endanger the health of my fellow citizens, I would like to ask the Minister whether he intends to verify these allegations with his Quebec colleague and, if they are accurate, what does he intend to do to remedy this serious problem?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
subsubtopic: CONTAMINATION OF SOIL AND WATER IN THE ROUYN-NORANDA AND VAL-D'OR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are very concerned about the situation revealed by this study. I asked my officials to make the necessary checks and I intend to open discussions with my colleague, the Quebec Environment Minister, on this subject.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FINANCE
FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. There was a symposium on poverty in my riding recently. Research conducted by the Nipissing University revealed that one in every five children in my riding lived below the poverty line. That works out to roughly 4,000 children. My question is this. What can the parents of these thousands of children, where the household income of 900 of these children was less than $5,000 per year, expect from this Government in the Budget on April 27? What hope can be offered to the poorest of my constituents?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)

THE LATE JAMES EDGAR WALKER
speechtext:
I rise to share with the House sadness at the news of the death of James Edgar Walker, a former colleague and friend who was known by Canadians as Jimmy.
Jimmy was much loved in this place on all sides and in the community which he represented so ably here from 1962 to 1974,namely the riding of York Centre in North York which I now have the honour to represent.
Jimmy died in a hospital bed in Toronto on Wednesday. He was 77. His beloved wife Lillian and his sons John and James were close at hand. He came to the House in 1962, a veteran of World War II, and a veteran also of North York municipal politics, already well known and respected in our community of North York.
He filled many assignments here with distinction during his long career, but there is no doubt that the most difficult and challenging one was that of Chief Government Whip in the minority Liberal Government of Lester Pearson. Jimmy's assignment was bringing out the troops, often for surprise votes at all times of the week and at all times of the day, under unrelenting House rules, which have long since been repealed because of their inhumanity.
This assignment took its toll on Jimmy and that should be recounted here, as should his service to Prime Minister Trudeau as Parliamentary Secretary. I do not know of anyone around here today like Jimmy. In the days when social service was not a normal part of a Member of Parliament's job, he was deeply involved in problem-solving for his constituents. He cared for his people and their needs, and his colleagues here all benefited also from his friendliness, and from his availability to give advice and to help us. He was always optimistic and he was always positive. He spoke well of everybody.
I think that Jimmy could have been elected to this place forever, whatever stripe the Government happened to have. His decision to step down in 1974 and to encourage me to come back to Parliament in this seat, gave me an opportunity for which I will always be indebted to him. To his family, Lillian his beloved wife, to his sons John and James, we send our sympathy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE LATE JAMES EDGAR WALKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government of Canada I want to join with my hon. friend, the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), in paying tribute to a very dear friend and very outstanding and special Commoner, Jimmy Walker, who has departed. I concur with all the sentiments that have been expressed by the Hon. Member for York Centre. In so doing, I simply want to reinforce the fact that to me and I am sure to many others, Jimmy Walker was considered a very decent person and a very honourable man, one I would consider a friend.
I recall when I first came to the House in 1968, Jimmy Walker was one of the first Members to come across the floor to introduce himself. I learned at that time that he was born and raised in Vegreville and we became very, very close friends from that day hence. As the Hon. Member for York Centre had indicated, he was always there to lend a helping hand and to reach out, and he certainly did that for me. He was a friend. He was always helpful. He reached out to help other Hon. Members from all sides of the House. I think that was really one of the very basic qualities of Jimmy Walker. He really was that kind of a person, always seeking ways and means of helping people.
When I came here in 1968,1 presume his role as Whip was a little easier than it was during the minority years. Nonetheless, being a government Whip is never an easy job. He discharged that responsibility in a very exemplary fashion.
As a Member, he defended his principles and ideals with vigour but he did it with dignity and honour. We all come here as members of a certain political Party, but Jimmy was certainly not noted for his partisanship. He was veiy even- tempered and he was more interested in the final results. He set an example in maintaining the very highest and finest traditions of parliamentary democracy.
April 21, 1989

He was a great House of Commons man, he was a tremendous people person and he dedicated his life to helping people. He was a family man, he had a distinguished military career and he was a very successful business person. He was a great Canadian, but I think most of all, we can hold Jimmy Walker up as a clear example of what a Member of Parliament should be. In so many respects, I think he epitomized the finest qualities of a Member of Parliament.
On behalf of my Party, and I know on behalf of all Hon. Members, I join with colleagues opposite in expressing our deepest sympathy on his passing. He was a great Canadian who will be sadly missed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I would like to associate ourselves with the words of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) and say a few words about the passing of Jimmy Walker. The Leader of my Party, myself and those others of us in the NDP who knew him were very saddened to hear about his passing. He was a Member of Parliament from 1962 to 1974.
I can remember when I was first elected with the Hon. Member for Vegreville in 1968, Jimmy Walker was one of those friendly Members of Parliament who came across and made himself well known to members of other Parties. He was certainly very well liked and highly respected by those of us on the opposition side. I recall him being a conciliator, a bit of a peacemaker in terms of the operations of the House of Commons. He was the Parliamentary Secretary to Pierre Trudeau, and I think that showed the respect that the Prime Minister of the day and the Liberal Party of the time had for the conciliation abilities of Jimmy Walker.
If I remember correctly, Jimmy Walker was a progressive Liberal, a person concerned about the disadvantage in society and what he could do for people who were less fortunate. He retired in 1974, and as his successor said, there was no doubt that if he had run again in 1974, he would have won the seat. However, he retired to become a citizenship judge. Those of us who knew him will miss him.

Mr. Speaker, I would want to extend my personal condolences and those of my Party to his wife Lillian, his two sons James and John, and his seven grandchildren.
