speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the post-secondary education program, I would like to start by commenting on certain remarks made by the Leader of the NDP with respect to Mr. Yalden's report tabled last week. I think the Leader of the NDP, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), accurately summarized certain statements in Commissioner Yalden's report, which we have of course read very carefully.
I believe Mr. Yalden described a situation that does in fact exist. Unfortunately, I feel that he failed to mention certain improvements that have been made over the years. I also believe that although governments have made considerable efforts in recent years to deal with the situation, a great deal remains to be done, and that being understood, I partly agree with Commissioner Yalden's comments, and I am sure that in the months and years to come, there will be many opportunities to discuss these issues.

With respect to this particular subject of post-secondary education, I am obviously glad to have the opportunity to address this issue fully in the House today. It is plagued by serious misunderstandings. I hope that the remarks made here today will give all students, including the ones who are on the hunger strike, Members of the House, and all Canadians a much better understanding of the new policy and guidelines on Indian post-secondary education assistance.
I am obviously very concerned with respect to the hunger strikers. I know that they sincerely believe in the validity of their actions. I have asked them to believe in my desire to hear their views fully and to respond to them.
I believe that we are far closer on this issue than the controversy today suggests. We share common objectives and equally strong commitments to meeting them. Over the months ahead we can sit down and work out specific concerns with the program. Today I particularly want to focus on the program and the guidelines, and attempt to explain them fully, and to explain why changes were necessary and why they are beneficial.
The Government is proud of this program, as are Indian people of their graduates. We need to overcome the serious misunderstandings that have arisen and have now become so charged with emotion and controversy. I want to establish good communication, and an effective working relationship with Indian people on this issue. I hope that the debate in the House today can serve those

April 21, 1989

objectives. I want to reassure Indian people across the country who are concerned about this program that I recognize their concerns and have always been ready to discuss them. As I have indicated from the outset, I am ready to start a bilateral process as soon as possible to formally address these issues and other related ones.
We are facing difficult times. Several major issues face us. The Post-Secondary Education Assistance Program is one of the most important of those major issues. We have to deal with it. I know that education is the best way to heal the social malaise and physical hardship that now afflict too many Canadian Indians. I know that the greatest hope for strong, vital Indian communities in the future is education. I know that Indian people have the talent, will, and commitment to make education work for them. I know that last fact because assistance for Indian post-secondary education is one of the most successful programs the federal Government has ever undertaken.
Under the previous policy, the number of post-secondary students increased from 3,500 in 1977-78, when the E-12 guidelines were introduced, to some 15,000 in 1988-89. During the same period, the budget for this program grew from $9 million to close to $130 million. Nevertheless, even the most successful policies need updating and revising from time to time to meet changing needs and emerging trends.
In this case, there is a need to increase the number of successful graduates of the program. Further, there is a need to encourage more Indian graduates who are able to help make self-government and economic independence a reality for their people.
One year ago, my predecessor launched a consultation process to consider revisions to the previous policy. A draft policy proposal was sent to all regions of the country. We were committed to formulating a policy that met Indian needs and Indian aspirations.
The concerns and recommendations of these groups are reflected in the revised policy. For example, the old policy system of limiting the length of student support to a specific number of student months has been changed to a system which provides for up to five years for a four-year program, and up to four years for a three-year program.
Supply
The previous wide range of regionally determined rates of assistance has been replaced by a nationally consistent rate structure. Average rates provided to students in most categories under the old guidelines have been increased under the new policy.
The earlier draft policy identified only a $1,000 scholarship for studies for self-government and economic self-sufficiency. A strategic studies scholarship of up to $3,500 per year has been developed under the revised policy. An academic achievement scholarship has been added which is up to $1,000 annually for qualified students. A special allowance has been provided in high-rent cities for single parents with dependants, and married students with both dependent spouses and children. Tuition fees are now covered regardless of time spent in post-secondary education. One result is that there is no limit to the number of degrees for which tuition, books and supplies are provided.
Those are ways in which our consultations with Indian people have helped make this policy a vast improvement over the old policy. However, those are only part of the whole range of benefits that would be available to eligible students under the new policy.
To summarize all those benefits, I would like to underline the following. Complete tuition assistance is provided to eligible full-time and part-time students. This includes fees for registration, tuition, and the cost of books and supplies required for a particular course of studies. Full-time students who must live away from their permanent places of residence may qualify for travel grants back to their homes once every semester for themselves and any dependants who reside with them. Students living away from home will be eligible to receive monthly allowances to help cover their living expenses, for example, food, rent, hydro, daycare, calculated by the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto according to the costs of living in Toronto, which are higher than anywhere else in Canada. In addition, under certain circumstances provisions have been made for increased allowances in high-rent areas.
The following is an illustration of some examples of levels of assistance. A single student living away from home will receive a maximum monthly living allowance of $675. A married student with an employed spouse and three dependants will receive a maximum of $1,205 per month. A single-parent student with three dependants will receive a maximum of $1,355 per month, plus a rental supplement where applicable.

April 21, 1989
Supply
Students will be eligible to receive funding to complete community college diplomas, certificates, undergraduate degrees, Masters, Ph.D. or professional degrees. Student allowances will be provided for the official length of each successive academic program: three years for a three-year program, four years for a four-year program. An additional year may be provided for a particular student to complete a degree or diploma program at each level.
Therefore, successful students will experience no difficulty in obtaining support through all the academic levels to the conclusion of a professional degree in law or a graduate program such as a Master's degree or a Ph.D.
Administering organizations, bands, tribal councils, education authorities, or other Indian organizations may also offer special incentives to eligible students in addition to the allowances provided under the basic policy.
For example, academic achievement scholarships of up to $1,000 may be granted to community college or undergraduate students who attain an average B or higher. Strategic studies scholarships may be granted for undergraduate students which may be worth up to $3,500 to encourage them to follow courses such as commerce, public or business administration, economics, applied and physical sciences, mathematics, computer science, forestry or engineering, courses that would contribute directly to achieving self-government and economic self-reliance in Indian communities; and awards of up to $1,500 for full-time students enrolled in advanced or professional degree programs such as Master's or Ph.D. programs.
Under the new policy, those administering organizations will have an even greater opportunity to participate directly in the post-secondary education process.
The new policy is sufficiently flexible to allow administering organizations to establish their own operating procedures provided these are consistent with the policy and respect the maximum rates and limits of assistance. To ensure fairness and equitable treatment under the policy, administering organizations will have to have an appeal process in place. The new policy also requires the establishment of a student registry that will greatly improve the data base for the program.
We need to work together with administering groups to establish an improved system for research and data collection. Two-thirds of the program is managed by bands, tribal councils, education authorities and other Indian groups. It has been very difficult in the past, Mr. Speaker, to obtain full statistical information. Therefore, cost projections from year to year have been based on historical trends in expenditures rather than actual demand. We need better information in order to plan and to forecast demand and costs. Because the new policy relates to support for individual students, provides incentives and scholarships and has a rate structure based on individual student costs, the budget for this fiscal year has been set on those criteria. However, if the data indicate there should be changes in financial resources in the future, I am prepared and will ask Cabinet for increased financial resources for the coming years to meet those growing demands.
I would like now to say a few words about treaties. I recognize how strongly Indian people feel about treaties. For Indian people treaties are fundamental to their existence as a people. They represent the contract that the great chiefs and their people signed with the Crown. They form the basis of the historic relationship between Indian people and the federal Government. My Government respects and values that relationship and so provides elementary and secondary education to Indians who reside on reserves. This commitment has been formalized in the Indian Act. In fact, my Government goes beyond the Indian Act and provides educational and support services far beyond what is required by the law. Our support includes pre-kindergarten, kindergarten, and post-secondary programs. With our elementary and secondary education programs I believe that my Government is observing the full spirit and intent of the education references in the treaties, but I do not agree that post-secondary education is a treaty right.
We must strengthen our policy commitment to encourage Indian people to attend colleges and universities and to graduate with the skills that much of the rest of this country takes for granted, skills necessary to develop the special potential of this vital part of our population. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we must all maintain our strong support for this program and to improve it in every way possible.
April 21, 1989

I have indicated my willingness to review the specific terms of the new policy. We have approximately four months before the program becomes operational. We should use that time to correct any inequities in the new policy that together we can identify. If it is determined that more is required to complete the review, then we will determine it at that time and take more time if necessary.
I am willing to sit down with the chiefs and student representatives to design a bilateral process of consultation on post-secondary student assistance as they have requested. I believe that this policy is better than the previous one. However, there may be some areas where there could be further improvements, or areas where there are unintended inequities. I have stated from the beginning that I am prepared to look at these if they can be demonstrated.
In this great country we share, there is a tradition of democratic processes. These include discussion, negotiation and, yes, even criticism. The goal we all strive for is a fairer, more productive Canada for all its citizens and I am prepared to contribute to that and to obtain the appropriate means in order to ensure post-secondary education for our native people.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to thank the Elon. Member for his most reasonable comment. The intention from the very start is relatively clear. We want to pursue this very successful program in post-secondary education for Indian students. I believe the numbers speak for themselves. As we have already indicated on numerous occasions, it went from $4.2 million to a $130 million, and from 3,000 students to 15,000 students. We are committed to pursuing this program. We recognize also that education is a solution to improving the situation of our native people.
What I have indicated from the outset when I announced the policy, is that it would have to be reviewed regularly. What I have also announced and agreed to since then, is to establish a bilateral process in order to obtain the data that we absolutely need to establish on a year-to-year or on a five-year prediction, the needs that we are going to encounter, so that we can plan and receive the appropriate funds, in order to recognize and enhance this post-secondary education program. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Let me focus on the key issue in this debate. We have here a growing number of young Canadian Indians who want to go on to university and college, to improve their human condition, to get off the welfare merry-go-round, and to escape poverty, but the Government is putting restrictions on their ability to do this. That is the issue in this debate. The Government is doing this by capping the funds available for Indian post-secondary education, at a time when the Indian population is expanding and more Indians are qualifying for university. What kind of perverse logic is that? It is almost as if the Government would prefer to continue paying out welfare moneys rather than help people get off welfare.
In a recent article in The Globe and Mail by Peter Desbarats, the dean of journalism at the University of Western Ontario, Mr. Desbarats said the following: "For centuries we have been telling native people that educa-
Supply
tion is the road to self-reliance. As soon as they started to follow this advice in significant numbers we backed away from it. Surely, the impact of this type of hypocrisy on the Canadian native population will in the long run be more costly than the relatively small amount of money it will save".
In 1982-83 I had the good fortune to serve on the Special Committee for Indian Self-Government chaired by my former colleague, Keith Penner, the Member of Parliament for Cochrane-Superior. I say "good fortune" because during those two years we had the opportunity to travel across the country and to meet Indian people in all parts of this land, to visit their lands and to find out about their dreams and their ambitions. When we published our report in 1983, before making recommendations we catalogued some of the social conditions faced by Indian people in the country at that time. I would like to detail some of them.
In terms of child welfare the proportion of Indian children in care had risen steadily to more than five times the national rate-five times higher than the non-Indian population. In terms of housing, nearly 19 per cent of on-reserve homes had two or more families living in them, these conditions affecting 40 per cent of all status Indian families. Facilities: fewer than 40 per cent of Indian houses had running water, sewage disposal or indoor plumbing facilities. The national level of properly serviced houses is over 90 per cent. The average income of Indian people is one-half to two-thirds of the national average. The death rate, despite improvements over the past 10 years, is two to four times the rate for non-Indians. The infant mortality rate among Indian children is 60 per cent higher than the national rate. The life expectancy for Indian people is 10 years less than for non-Indian people.
That was in 1983. The conditions have not improved that much since that time. If we look at the report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, which was published just a few weeks ago, we see that Mr. Yalden stated: "The situation faced by Canada's native peoples is in many ways a national tragedy. The grand promise of equality of opportunity that forms the central purpose of the Canadian Human Rights Act stands in stark contrast to the conditions in which many native people live".

April 21, 1989
Supply
Mr. Yalden went on to state: "Native peoples are drastically under-represented in employment in virtually every industrial sector and eveiy occupation, even in locations like Winnipeg or Regina where there is a high concentration of natives. Within federal government Departments themselves, where programs to promote native hiring have been in place for some time now, the representation of native peoples is abysmal in all but the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs". Those are the social conditions that are facing the native people of Canada.
I spoke a moment ago about the dreams and ambitions of Indian people. I just want to refer Hon. Members to a special study that was done with respect to our Indian people by The Free Press of Winnipeg on October 14, 1988. In carrying out this study the newspaper conducted an inquiry among Indian children as to what their ambitions might be. I would like to quote from some of the letters that were sent in by Indian children on the reserves.
Anne, a 13-year old girl, wrote: "When I grow up I would like to be a store manager and I would like to help the old people find what they want. First I will finish my education and go on to high school and university. Then after that I would come home and be a store manager".
Linda, 12 years old, wrote: "I would like to be a police girl because I do not like people getting drunk and if they do I will make sure they are not getting hurt and my family will be very proud of me, of being a cop, that I will be a cop forever and I will never break one rule. I won't drink".
Candice, who is 11 years old, wrote: "When I get out of school I will go to school at Brandon University. I am planning to be a teacher when I grow up. My Mom is a teacher".
The citations by young Indian people with respect to their ambitions and with respect to their dreams goes on.
One must not forget in this debate that in the last Parliament we passed Bill C-31 which greatly added to the number of status Indians in Canada. The estimate is that the number of people who have been added to the rolls of status Indians as a result of that law is between
30,000	to 80,000. We cannot get an exact figure, but it is relatively high.
In the debate so far there seems to be some confusion on the government side with respect to capping. Some have said that there is no cap. Then, earlier this morning in answer to questions from the Leader of the NDP the
Minister admitted that there is a cap. There is a limit on the amount of money available to the students for post-secondary education. No one has said that the Government has cut back on the funding. We have not said that. Of course there have been increases in the funding. However, there has been a limit on the increases in the funding. The increases have not been sufficient to cover those people who are qualified for university and accepted by universities.
I would now like to refer to a brief that was sent to us by the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians who stated: "The new policy and guidelines would create undue hardships for Indian students. The capping of the funds available, combined with demographic realities that accelerate demand for post-secondary education by Indian students, would severely limit the financial resources available on a per-student basis, and effect a reduction in the numbers and success rates of students enrolled in universities, and other post-secondary institutions already under-represented by 50 per cent in comparison to enrolment rates of the general Canadian society. Indian participation in post-secondary education should be promoted and increased, helping to raise, not lower, the proportion of Indians in post-secondary education".
With respect to this capping, as I have said, there is some misunderstanding. Perhaps I could put it this way for purposes of the Government and the public. Let us consider a program such as Old Age Security. Under that program when someone turns 65 he or she receives Old Age Security, whatever the fixed amount is. No matter if the health rates improve or if the population increases, as soon as someone turns 65 and no matter what the numbers are, they all receive Old Age Security. We do not say to them: "There is only a budget of so much and, unfortunately, the budget level has been reached and now we must reduce the Old Age Security. It is first in, first served". We have a program which states that no matter how many people turn 65 they will receive the old age security pension. That is a program without limit, without a cap.
In the program that is put before us and what the Minister is doing is putting a limit on the amount of moneys available for Indians in post-secondary education. He is saying that they will only be admitted into the program up to the point of reaching that limit. What we are saying, and what the Indians are saying, is that all Indian students who are qualified and are accepted to university should have the right to go to university without limit.
April 21, 1989

This is not a great number of people. It is increasing, certainly, and I mentioned the figures in that regard. However, the total number of Indians and aboriginal people is at most one million. A few years ago we had about 300,000 status Indians. Perhaps that number has gone up to 400,000. There are 15,000 Indian students in post-secondary education. In the City of Montreal we have more students in post-secondary education than 15,000. That is not a great number. So perhaps there is another 1,000 or another 2,000. Surely a rich country such as Canada can afford to pay for that. There should be no capping with respect to these people.
I do not doubt the Minister's sincerity, but he is part of a Government. He is subject to the restraints of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and so on. When he is enunciating a policy, he has to enunciate it in the context of what they will permit. Unfortunately, it is a very narrow approach that they are taking. Those young people who are risking their lives in this hunger fast have not been risking their lives for nothing. They are risking their lives because they understand that they will not be able to get the education they need. That is a serious matter.
Once again, I say there should be no cap. All those Indian students who are qualified and accepted by universities should be given the financing necessary to pursue their studies. The alternative open to them, Mr. Speaker, is welfare. When I was sitting with the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government, we heard people asking, Why should there be a special program for Indian post-secondary education? Why should they have a program that is different from any that we non-Indians have? The answer, Mr. Speaker, is that such a program is part of our settlement with the native people, with the aboriginal people, for occupying this land that once was all theirs. At one time, all this land that is now Canada was the land of the aboriginal people: the land, the water, the mines, the resources, the oil, the gas. It was all theirs. We came from Europe and elsewhere and occupied the land in great numbers, and very often pushed them off to the less productive lands.
Supply
In turn for taking a lot of their land, we made agreements, sometimes in treaties, sometimes not in treaties, on the basis of their aboriginal rights to pay them back for that land. We have not paid very much. Part of the pay-back is funding for post-secondary education. If we look at the result of the takeover of this land by the European peoples, who is rich and who is poor? The people who owned the land in days gone by are certainly not the rich people. They are not controlling this country and this land. So the least we can do is have a generous program for education, especially postsecondary education. This is small payment for the lands that we took, lands which are making most of us rich. That is a small compensation that we who have come from European stock and other stock can pay to these people who once owned and occupied all of this land.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say this. In a recent report on aboriginal justice, it was pointed out that a native child today has a better chance of ending up in jail than receiving a university degree. George Erasmus, the President of the Assembly of First Nations, has pointed out that there is no cap on native welfare programs, but there is going to be a cap on native education programs. It will be far cheaper in the long run to help Indian people with their education than to perpetuate the cycle of welfare and dependence. In considering these matters, I would ask the Minister and the Government to reconsider their foolish policy of limiting this money for our Indian people.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member enjoys quoting from The Globe and Mail. I would also like to quote an editorial from The Globe and Mail of April 20, 1989, where it states, "We have trouble finding Ottawa's position unreasonable". The Globe and Mail goes on to say that "the principle of imposing a budget on the program and making students more accountable for completing their degrees within a reasonable amount of time is not the ogre its critics make it out to be."
I would like to know how the Hon. Member can argue that the program has been capped or that it has been decreased when it has been increased so significantly.

April 21, 1989
Supply

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Obviously the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary was not listening to me. At no time did I say the Government has cut back on the program. They have not. They have increased the program. We admit that. But they have not increased the program to the limits that are necessary, and they have put a cap on. That is clear in the letter that was written by the Minister to the Chiefs of Canada. This was quoted earlier by the leader of the NDP and by my colleague. It said:
The time has come for a major reappraisal to determine how the program could produce larger numbers of graduates within a budget that could not continue to grow at the pace of the last decade.
They are increasing the budget, but they are increasing it with a cap on it. The Hon. Member referred to The Globe and Mail. The Globe and Mail congratulates the Government for putting a cap on it-that great Tory newspaper. In an editorial of April 20 headlined "Native students and higher education", they say:
This month, Ottawa did to this assistance program what it has done, or will be doing, to other programs it finances. It set a global budget for the spending, to control expenses and impose some discipline on students taking advantage of the program.
So The Globe sees that they are doing that and congratulates them for it. I do not agree with The Globe, Mr. Speaker. What we are saying is that this is not the kind of program where there should be a limit. This should be like the old age security program. In the old age security system, if you turn 65 you qualify and the Government has to provide the money. We are saying that if you are an Indian student and you qualify for university and you are accepted, you should get the money.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always found my hon. friend for Notre-Dame-de-Grace to be very reasonable. We have served on committees together on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I find it difficult to understand why he continually refers to a budget item as a cap. He says it should work exactly the same way as old age security. I know he recognizes that when budgeting takes place in the Department responsible for old age security, we have the data, we have the figures, we know what to budget for, as his Government did, and as our Government has done. What we are budgeting for is old age security. How much is the Government going to spend? With the best available data that the Indian Affairs Department had, they budgeted $130 million for post-secondary education feeling that they had covered every student. This was the budget. This is what they felt
was needed for every student who qualifies for post-secondary education to be included within that $130 million.
The problem that we are having is getting all of the data together. That is the push that the Department is trying to make now, to gather the data together. Surely, the Hon. Member does not believe that we should just submit a zero figure, or a question mark, when we are budgeting. Surely he does not believe that. It has to be a budget item. That is what it is, a budget item. It is not a cap. If the budget is out, it will be increased the following year.
If the budget is too much the following year, it will be reduced. But we need the co-operation of the bands who administer the funds in most cases. We need to have the figures on those students who are streaming in. If you go to any school board, they budget. If you go to any university institution, they budget. That is what we are talking about; it is a budget. It is not a cap. If more money is needed, more money will be put in the budget. That is what it amounts to, and I would ask him to comment on that.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the Minister and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development do not have full control over that matter. Even if their forecasts were good and they could forecast exactly how much money they would need for all the Indian students who might be qualified for university, they have to go Treasuiy Board, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Privy Council Office. I served in that particular ministry. I know.
We also know that right now the priority of the Government is to cut the deficit. It will be making cut-backs in all kinds of departments. It is the Government that budgeted. We do not know whether that is what the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development recommended. All we know is what has come from the Government. It has budgeted an amount of money that many people say is inadequate.
For example, Chairman Beth Brown, president of the Canadian Student Federation said that under the old policy, enrolment of native students in post-secondary schools rose to about 15,000 from 2,500 in 1974. She says that the restraints that are being proposed means that 1,100 students would not be able to attend college or university in September. That is what the president of the Canadian Federation of Students says.
April 21, 1989

I also remind the Member that in the days when our baby boom children were going to school, we did not put a limit or cap on our public school system.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: We had a budget.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: If there were children ready to go to school, we built the schools, hired the teachers and made sure they had a place to go to school. We did not say that because of the budget it is too bad, that child got in first and that kid cannot come in. There was universal access to education at the public level. We took care of all the children who wanted to go to school. That is what should be done with native people in this country.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
I am sure my Liberal colleague has noted the difference between referring to The Globe and Mail in respect of a news report and referring to The Globe and Mail in terms of support for Tory policy and ignoring what Indian journalists might say in their newspapers about their rights.
It cannot have been missed by anyone that there are any number of programs which exist without caps. Nobody questions the necessity of having budgets, but budgets are always over-run on the basis of supplementary estimates when it is found that the cost exceeds what was budgeted. For instance, as prisons expand, the ones that incarcerate Indians and others in the population, there are infinite funds for that. Of course, there is the Canada Assistance Program which feeds the welfare budgets of our municipalities all across this land. No one has ever said that should be capped. Indeed, one might recall that there should have been a bloody cap on the amount of this country that was taken from the Indians in the first place.
Does my hon. colleague not believe that it is more than fair to have a program which will make it possible for every aboriginal person to have access to post-secondary education? After all, they gave a whole country away in order to have it.

Mr. Speaker, that is what I thought I had said, but I appreciate the vigorous way in which it was seconded by my hon. friend, the Member for Windsor- Lake St. Clair (Mr. McCurdy).

He referred to my citation of an editorial in The Globe and Mail. The only reason I did that was to indicate to the Government that it is not only the Opposition Parties that know there is a cap being applied. The Globe and Mail, the Government's great supporter, also recognizes that a cap is being put on. The Globe and Mail, because of its small "c" conservative policies, congratulates it for the cap. We do not congratulate the Government for the cap. There is a place for caps in some types of budgets which vary from year to year.
I point out again that the path to self-reliance for our Indian people is through education. The way for them to get beyond those social conditions that were described to us when we travelled throughout this country is through education. The way to do it is through education, and we should be more than generous in assisting that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate. In my nine years in public life, I have never found that debates in this House have done anything more than inform Canadians and give them both sides of the story. I think it particularly helps the Government to set out all the facts and give the background on an issue. It gives greater balance to Canadians who are discussing the issue, whatever it might be.
We come from a huge country, with many interests being represented. This Parliament administers and allocates $132 billion. In each one of those interests and those budgetary allocations there are strongly held views that there should be more or should be less, or that new programs should be established and existing programs should be cut. This is where that entire process takes place and where the final decisions are made. That is the nature of democracy and the nature of government in Canada today.
Today we are dealing with the issue of native education. I happen to represent, as part of my riding, the largest Indian reserve in the land. It is one of the most progressive native communities in this country. They are great farmers and great ranchers. A few weeks ago an agreement on an irrigation project was signed to help irrigate their land and produce food, not only for Canada but the world. That is a genuine achievement of a band that is ready for self government in every way. If I had my way, they would have a lot more of it than they do today, but even on that issue within the blood group itself not everyone is in agreement with the concept of self government. It is necessary to meet, talk and debate.

April 21, 1989
Supply
I believe all Members are concerned about the specific students who are on a hunger strike. In a free democratic society that is not the way to show one's concern or point of view. Certainly, one is free to do that. In a society, one is free not to eat. One is free to starve to death if one wishes, but that is not the way we ought to do it.
In this vast country with its many interests, everyone would do that if it were a strategy to which governments would succumb. We are multicultural. Immigrant groups could be starving to death. Refugee groups could be starving to death. Some of us feel strongly about the entrenchment of property rights. Some feel strongly enough that they would starve for that right, just as some of our ancestors fought and died to get the entrenchment of property rights in their constitutions. There are people who feel very strongly about both sides of the abortion issue.
The fundamental point to determine is how a society resolves that. In a totalitarian state that is controlled by one party, the party will make the decision while the citizen has no say. In a totalitarian state with a military junta, a few generals will make the decision. In a monarchy, a family compact will make the decision. However, in our western world where we have a democracy, the citizens elect 295 people to come here. We have strongly held political views which sometimes cross Party lines, but this is where the issue must be resolved. Not only we as Members but the Government itself is accountable to the people every four or five years.
Personally, I do not believe that hunger strikes are the way to pressure for change. I therefore sincerely urge the students to stop their hunger strike and meet the Minister. I believe other Members should be encouraging that as well.
I believe the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) should have stood in the House and rejected this method as the way to resolve the issue. They should have asked the students to give up their hunger strike, to talk with them so that their views could be presented within the parliamentary process. They did not do that. I think they took advantage of these young students on this particular issue.
Let us deal with the program involved in this issue. It is a program of enormous success. When we came to government, some $50 million to $54 million was being spent on the program. This year the amount is $130 million. In the last four years, when other programs have received less, this program has more than doubled, as it should because of the success that the native students are achieving at the high school level. They are qualifying to go on to college and university.
Once students, native and non-native, graduate from high school and decide to go to post-secondary education, all are subsidized up to about 90 per cent in terms of the cost of that university. For natives and non-natives, all of that tuition is subsidized. Non-native students pay for their books, their travel, their room and board, their clothing and all of the rest of it. This program provides for natives something that non-natives are not entitled to. This was a policy decision made by this Parliament and I think it is a wise policy decision, one which I am prepared to talk to non-native students about.
There are many, many thousands of non-native students who come from families that are desperately poor. In some families, the fathers, mothers, sisters and brothers work to help those young people get through university and college. For native students, we use the Consolidated Revenue Fund to help them.
I do not believe that anyone in this Parliament is opposed that policy. We believe that these funds should be set aside so that natives get tuition fees and books and supplies for their whole life if they wish to go to university that long. There is no limit to funding for tuition, books and supplies. There is a limit for the extra expenses of transportation, day care, room and board and the like.
The policy provides that a native student can have up to five years to finish a course that most would finish in four years. Again, that is because of the unique situation from which they come. For a three-year course, they can have up to four years. That is not unreasonable, but I submit that Hon. Members ought to consider that there is a possible defect in this when it comes to the Charter of Rights.
If a non-native student were to bring a Charter action under the equality section against that policy, who knows what a court would ultimately do. This would mean that society would either have to provide this funding for all students, native or non-native, and some might want that to happen, or else it would have to cut the program out entirely.
April 21, 1989

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Read the Charter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
My friend is no doubt referring to affirmative action, but we never know if a court will go along with that. Is it fair to non-native students who come from desperately poor families that native students receive this funding and they do not? A court might find that to be not equal treatment, in which case the program would either be totally lost or would have to be provided for everyone. Even members of the NDP realize that there is not enough money in society to provide that degree of help for every student, native or non-native.
There are other issues at play as well. There is the question of self-government. It is my own personal view, and I believe it is the policy of Parliament, that natives should move to self-government as quickly as they themselves can be ready for it. That is why under the program there is an extra supplement for natives who will take programs that will assist in self-government and in self-management of the reserves. That is a good policy. I personally believe that self-government is a good policy and we should be pushing it forward more quickly.
There is also the question as to whether or not post-secondary education is a treaty right. Natives have always held the view that it is and are pushing it vigorously. I do not believe that there is a Party in this House or in the country that has ever adopted the position that post-secondary education is a treaty right. Is that the view of Members of the NDP? I do not think they have formulated that policy.
The Liberals formed the Government for many years and we all have a policy for giving extra assistance to natives, but I do not believe it is a Party policy that post-secondary education is a treaty right. To the extent that Hon. Members are misleading natives on that, they are not correct. They should not be doing that. It is not fair to do so unless a Party is prepared to state that that is its policy. If it is, that policy should be announced so the Canadian people may judge it.
Members of the Opposition are using the political cliche of a cap on the budget. It is a very effective tool that Members of the Opposition have adopted, and I praise them for it. When we were in opposition, we tried
Supply
to use those little cliches that would crystallize things, and so they are using the word "cap" as if the program had been capped. That is nonsense.
Indeed, we as Members of Parliament have an obligation to budget properly and to account for that budget. In this case, two thirds of the post-secondary education budget is operated by agencies not attached to the Department but by native agencies themselves. To make an annual budget, the Department makes estimates and then spends them. If the money runs out, it comes back for supplementary estimates.
We as a Government have an obligation, but Members of the Opposition do too. Are they calling for wide open spending without knowing how many students are involved and how the money is spent? If that is what they are advocating, that is irresponsible to the Canadian public as a whole. We have an obligation to account for the money and that is what the policy does. The Minister has quite properly taken that view. Give us the data. If there are more students and they need help, we will go to Cabinet and to Parliament with supplementary estimates.
Members of the Opposition are saying that they do not need data, that they do not care how many students there are. They are saying that if these agencies want $200 million, we should give them $200 million. Is that really what opposition Members are saying? Of course it is not, because they are responsible Members of Parliament as well and have to account to the public.
I would like to deal further with the role of the Opposition. It is proper for us to have strongly held views that may differ. However, on one issue we should all be unanimous, and that is in the way we express dissent in a democracy. I would like opposition Members to ask publicly if they believe that a hunger strike is the way to go. Why have they not asked those young students that question? They should encourage those students to talk to them, they should offer to help them present their case and then hope they will vote for them in the next election. However, they should say that in a democracy, with great respect, we do not starve to death. That is not an appropriate way to do it, because if everyone does that, our whole society will go into a state of chaos. I would like opposition Members to rise and tell us their view on that point.

April 21, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I am quite disappointed in the statement of the Hon. Member. Obviously he did not listen to what the Minister said. He did not listen to the admission of the Minister that the Government failed in establishing a data base to obtain statistics pertaining to the program. The Hon. Member also said that 90 per cent of fees for all students across Canada is paid by the Government. Is that an accurate figure?
I was disappointed that the Hon. Member spoke of education as being related to a treaty. In my view, education is the right of every Canadian, native or non-native. The educational system should be revamped to the point where there would be no differentiation between native and non-native students. If that means that the Government should invest more in education, then let it do so because that is the only way to go.
The Hon. Member said that Members of the Opposition should call on the Indians to stop their hunger strike. It is not our duty to tell those students what to do. They know best what to do. Now it looks as if the Minister is indicating that he seems to be coming to an agreement to at least discuss the matter.
I must commend the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) for admitting honestly to the House the failure of the Government over the past four years to address the issue and to set up a proper support program. Mr. Speaker, I suppose I reciprocate the Hon. Member's disappointment. I am quite disappointed in his so-called question or comment, because I thought he would have understood far more than he appears to have done.
I must say that the Hon. Member's election brought us some glee. We wish we could have had a Conservative elected in Ottawa Centre, but at least the man he defeated was a thorn in our sides, and we welcome the Hon. Member as an alternative to the former Member.
The policy has always been subject to change. I think the Hon. Member got sucked into this capping argument, that somehow there was a sum of money that would never increase and was fixed for all time. That was
never the purpose. I will grant that members of the Opposition led Canadians to believe it, and many do believe it. However, that simply was never correct. In the second last paragraph of his letter announcing the policy, the Minister made it clear that it would always be subject to review. However, we need the data.
Are members of the Liberal Party saying that the Minister should be allocating unlimited resources to two-thirds of the agencies that administer this policy, without having any checks or balances, without knowing how many students, or without knowing how much is spent on room and board? That is irresponsible.
If Members opposite are not saying that, what is their criticism? If we have the data which shows that more students require it, then the program will be increased.

The Hon. Member was very careful to draw a picture which contrasts the treatment accorded to native people in terms of free post-secondary education with the situation for the rest of the population. Member thinks that this is unjust, or whether he was attempting to draw divisions between native people and the rest of the population and suggesting that it was unfair for the majority that native people should be accorded this. Member that we do not talk to native people because they are going to vote for us. We talk to them because we believe in what they believe in, in terms of justice.
April 21,1989	COMMONS

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commence my remarks by saying how proud I am to be a Canadian, and how proud I am to be a Member of the House representing 8,000 Indian children in the riding of Prince Albert-Churchill River. I say it is historic because even though the issues may seem relatively small, that they are just some departmental guidelines, they have come to symbolize the gulf that exists between this Government and the aboriginal people as to what the historic obligations of the Government of Canada are. I also say it is historic because for many Canadians who do not have the opportunity of close contact with the Indian and Inuit communities, this is the first time there has been enough media coverage of a major issue of importance to the Indian community for them to know what is going on.
As I was going through my files on this issue, I realized that I first became aware of this matter in May of 1988 when the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) answered my request for a copy of a purported Government document known as the Buffalo Jump Plan, an internal document of January 19, 1988, from the Department of Indian Affairs. This document has some very interesting things in it that are germane to this debate. Under communications, it outlines what the Government is supposed to say as it implements this plan. It says:
Confirm the themes of-we honour our commitments, we're fair, we are making progress. We're not seeking dramatic change, but rather to be fair and businesslike. When it can be done it will. Both for Indian and general audiences, it is good to emphasize the fairness theme: it's fair that Indians be well educated, fair that Indians take charge of looking after their own children, fair that the Indians govern themselves.
Those are the fine soothing words the Government is instructed to use to cover up what comes next.
What does come next in this document? First, no to C-31:
Be prepared to stick with C-31 as it is.
That is where the Government took on its obligation to provide funding for the people coming into the treaty under Bill C-31. Here the Government says no. Section 14 says that there will be fewer schools. It says:
We can build better schools, but fewer. Need to consult so as to balance the good news ("better") with the bad news ("fewer"). Should get our material out before AFN tables their long-promised report on Indian education.
They are playing games with that issue. Then we get into child abuse. It reads:
Cannot avoid support on child abuse, since anyone would see this as part of "basic care".
What they are talking about doing is going to the Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan, redirecting off-reserve welfare assistance to provide funding for better child care services in those provinces.
The situation is so bad and the Government is so concerned on that one that it is prepared to take money from social assistance rather than big corporations to use it to counter the problem of child abuse. Then we get to the Student Grants Program. Here we see the first hint of what is happening:
Agree to consultation in 1988, for implementation of amended program criteria in 1989.
This is the pre-election program of the Government.
Important to sustain rate of funding increase in 1988-89 while consultation proceeds.
So we have a scam here. What the Government has done is artificially inflate the 1988-89 budget to come up with that figure of $130 million so that it looks like the Government is being very generous and so people would not notice when the Government starts its capping and cutting and whatever else it is planning to do with the new guidelines, which means that there is no longer a treaty obligation to provide post-secondary education. That is why the Indian and Inuit people feel so strongly about the issue. They feel strongly about it because they know what is happening with post-secondary education guidelines. They know that is part of the Government's plan and it is the Government's plan they have to stop and stop now. They have to stop this plan because it
April 21, 1989

directly threatens them with having to go to court to get their treaty rights recognized.
Let me go to another section of this document where it reads:
Wish to proceed under Treaty Land Entitlement. Wish to proceed pragmatically (no announcements) with selected negotiations based on land entitlements to date of first survey. Not prepared to go further unless forced to by courts eventually.
If eventually somebody takes this to the court the Government is prepared to talk about treaties but not until that time. That is why the people in the Indian world see these guidelines as being so sinister. It is because they are part of this plan and no one has told them that this is not the plan of the Government. In fact, they have reason to believe, as we do, that it is the plan of the Government.
I think this all goes back to the basic constitutional framework of this country. The Minister made what I think is an appalling statement when he said that he unilaterally felt that post-secondary education was not a treaty right. It is not the job of the Minister or of any Minister or any individual or any Party to determine what are the treaty rights in this country. Section 35 of the Constitution Act of this country states that those rights will be determined in consultation, in negotiation, formal nation to nation consultation between the Governments of Canada and the Governments of the First Nation. That is the only way you can determine what treaty rights are. For two years the Government has had that particular consultation on hold.
Perhaps it might be worthwhile to go through some of these historic obligations to show that this is not just some archaic or arcane type of document that someone filed some place in the distant past. It says some very important things. Reading from The Royal Proclamation:
-the several Nations or THbes of Indians with whom We are connected and, who live under our Protection, should not be molested or disturbed in the Possession of such Parts of Our Dominions and Territories as, not having been ceded to or purchased by Us, are reserved to them, or any of them, as their Hunting Grounds.
Supply
I think that is very germane also to the Innu issue, if I may digress, where it says that they will not be molested or disturbed on their lands until their lands have been formally ceded or bought. That is something that has not happened. This is what commits the Government to making treaties. It also says:
We have thought proper to allow Settlement: but that, if at any Time any of the Said Indians should be inclined to dispose of the Said Lands, the same shall be Purchased only for Us, in our Name, at some public Meeting or Assembly of the Said Indians, to be held for that Purpose by the Governor or Commander in Chief of our Colony respectively within which they shall lie-conformable to such Directions and Instructions as We or they shall think proper to give for that Purpose -
In other words, when this land is ceded there are instructions which either they or the Government, the Indian people or the Government, lay down in treaty and they then become part of the constitutional framework of this country. The Government either does not know that or is totally ignoring it.
That brings us back to the now infamous guidelines. The Indian people are convinced on the basis of the treaties which do exist that post-secondary education is an obligation of the Canadian Government which they pre-paid with their land. It is a pre-paid obligation. There is no such thing as this being subject to a budgetary whim of this House. It is a pre-paid obligation which they paid for by allowing their lands for settlement.
Further to that, all the numbered treaties that I have read, and I believe I have read them all, state specifically that education is a treaty right. The Commissioner who signed those treaties said in his comments on the treaty that what he meant by that and what he had agreed to was that the Indians would have access-in the words he used, "the cunning of the white man". There can be no other interpretation of that, I believe, in the framework of 1989 than to mean that this means post-secondary education, because that is how you happen by "the cunning of the white man". That is why the potential threat of budgetary limits is so alarming to the Indian community. A budgetary limit would mean that what is theirs by constitutional right would suddenly become subject to the budgetary mercies of the government of the day. With this Government, in the post-free trade environment in which we live with big business on a rampage, there is no good reason why the Indian people of this country should have any faith or confidence in the budgetary mercies of this Government.

April 21, 1989
Supply

speechtext: Or anybody else.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Or anybody else for that matter. I do not have time to go into all the details of what is wrong with the guidelines. Those have been discussed very well elsewhere by Sharon Ironstar and others of the fasters, by the Indian leadership, by other colleagues in this House and the co-ordinated action across the country which some of us who have been here have not been aware of, but there has been an extensive program of education across Canada, and those have dealt with many of the issues, as has the Minister.
I would like to zero in on two myths, the soothing language which has become the heart of the Government's defence in this issue. First is the myth of generosity. The Government has made much of how generous it is being in these post-secondary guidelines which it is coming in with now. I would point out that some former colleagues of mine in private life-I did research into these issues-did an analysis of these guidelines for the Prince Albert District Chiefs and they found in the guidelines the proposed increases from 1982 to 1989 represented an increase of 6 per cent to 10 per cent over 1982 levels. That is 25 per cent less than the rate of inflation over that period of time. It leaves every one of these people under the nationally defined poverty level. Although there is perhaps no big argument that some of these allowances are in fact adequate, many of them are not. It certainly is wrong to describe this as generous. It is not. It is niggardly.
Then there is the myth of consultation. I enjoyed speaking to the rally on Friday afternoon on the Hill-

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Shame, shame!

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
-and describing to the people my brush with this Government's consultation process. The consultation process that I experienced happened as follows: On December 16, representatives of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations met with us and presented us with their arguments and documents, outlining point by point what is wrong with these guidelines and the consultation process, and asking for our commitment to do something about it. On behalf of the Saskatchewan New Democrats in this House, I wrote a letter to the then Minister of Indian Affairs, the Hon. Bill McKnight, in which I pointed out:
The proposed changes totally ignore the fact that the issues involved are addressed directly in Treaties between the Indian people and the Crown, and they cannot be addressed in a unilateral fashion.
That is what I did, and what my colleagues did. We were very surprised when we met for the first time with the Indian students and they hauled out the list of people that had been consulted. There on the list was the Saskatchewan NDP caucus. This is the consultation. We wrote them a letter saying we fundamentally disagree and the Government is saying that they consulted with us. No wonder the Indian people in this country think this was a bogus process. It was a bogus process. I know that.
Maybe the Minister who is caught in the middle of this mess should consider who it actually is that is holding him hostage. Is it the Indian students, or is it the people that penned the infamous "Buffalo Jump" document and committed the Government to this suicidal course of action? I believe he is being held hostage by somebody other than the students. I believe that the people who wrote the "Buffalo Jump" are the people who are holding the Minister hostage.
Allow me to summarize my remarks by repeating that I believe the evidence which says that post-secondary education for the original people of this country is a constitutional obligation of the Government of Canada, and the Minister has no unilateral right to change that.
I believe these guidelines represent an abrogation of this historic and constitutional obligation. But by way of trying to contribute constructively to this process, and realizing it has been difficult for a lot of people, particularly the Minister who is caught in it, I tried on Friday to table a five-point program which, if the Minister were to accept it, would lead to a rapid resolution of this issue. Hopefully, the Minister will still do that.
That is why I stand in the debate to support this motion. I think it makes economic sense to not proceed with these guidelines because we are talking about future burdens on future taxpayers of this country. There is no greater burden on the future taxpayers than to save $30,000 to educate a person now and then have to pay $500,000 in welfare over the next 65 years. It makes budgetary, fiscal and economic sense to not proceed with these guidelines and to have a bilateral process of consultation, because that is what the Constitution obligates us to do. If we are going to do that, it makes sense to not proceed with these guidelines until such time as that consultation is complete.
April 21, 1989

In conclusion, I would like to take a moment to recognize the contribution of other people to this debate. I would like to acknowledge my many teachers through the years, particularly the Indian people I have known who have taught me their ways. I would like to thank the Indian leadership and the students for being open, honest and very forthcoming in our discussions with them. I would like to thank my colleagues in the NDP caucus, because I believe we have exemplified what team work can do in bringing an issue before the people of Canada. I would also like to thank all other Hon. Members on this side of the House and the other side who have taken a serious enough interest in this issue that we are having this debate. I would finally like to acknowledge the Indian children of this country. It is because of their hopes for the future that all of this is worth it.

I thank the Hon. Member for the opportunity to clarify my intention in the remarks that I made. I do not believe that I said there was no money for post-secondary education under the Bill C-31 program. I know there was money in that program, and I did not mean to suggest otherwise. What I did mean to suggest was that there is a general pattern of implementation of the infamous "Buffalo Jump'' document. What I said is prepared to stick with C-31 as it is, no amendments before the next election, possible commitment or minor adjustments later. I believe that is the policy of the Government, that there has not been new money under C-31.
While we are talking about C-31, in many ways it crystallizes some of these issues. In my own constituency there are 5,000 people in the C-31 category that are living in no-man's land. The Government has granted them status but there has been no parallel provision for them to be absorbed into the bands which they want to belong to. The bands are reluctant to be pushed into this because there is no money for them to provide the services which those people then come to expect. That is one of the sinister aspects of these guidelines. If there is a budgetary limit, if in fact the first 15,000 get funding and the next 2,000 have to wait until next year, the pressure is on those bands to determine who will get that money and who will not. The presence in my constituency of 5,000 C-31 people just increases those pressures and makes it that much worse.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the Minister that if I am ever part of a Government it will not be because I have crossed the floor.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
For the information of the Minister, although I did not deal with the specific reference to guidelines in the document, I was referring to a scenario which I think is quite clear.
The scenario is that in fact the Government would be seeking what might be considered to be an inflated level of funding in the election year and that the consultation process would proceed against that backdrop. I contend that that was an unrealistic impression the Government was trying to leave, and not a totally accurate one. We have seen the results of that as the figure of $130 million is repeatedly pointed to as an indication of how fast this has increased in the past.
With reference to the consultation process, I agree with the Minister that it is useful to listen to dissenting views. However, to be considered part of a process that the Government takes some pride in-in fact to call it consultation-when someone writes the Minister a letter, is not accurate.
I would assume that consultation would include some back and forth, that the Government would provide us with some information and that we would get back to the Government with some information and so on. That was not the case. I was surprised that on the basis of one
letter we should be listed as having been involved in the consultative process, along with the Assembly of First Nations, the Prince Albert District Chiefs, the Inuit Tapirisat and all the other people. If this is how we had been consulted I was left to wonder how they had been consulted. Indeed, the Indian leadership and the students say that they have not been consulted.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does my hon. colleague agree that this new attack, what some perceive to be a new attack, is part of a Tory strategy which has been ongoing for several years and that we are seeing the usual shell games trying to cover up real budget cuts?
Does he think that this indeed relates to the over-all philosophy of the Conservative Government which is that it has abandoned the very concept of universal access for natives?
I would like to give one illustration from my riding of Vancouver East which many native people say is the largest reserve in Canada. The Native Education Centre in my riding serves students from all over British Columbia. It does an outstanding job in both academic upgrading and in practical courses, as well as in programs for native training. There is a course for native child care workers, administrators for bands, as well as people training in high technology of different kinds. The institution has had a very good success rate with highly motivated students who attend regularly.
In 1987 the budget of the institution from DIA was $125,000. In 1987-88 that budget was cut by 60 per cent. The next year there were no funds at all for a very major educational institution which has made a terrific contribution to the education of native people in British Columbia. As a result of a very strong process in which a number of us were involved, the Government found $82,000 in 1989.
I would like to point out where the money for this came from. The Government took the money out of moneys that were designated for students. That is what I mean when I say a shell game. I wish I had time to give the rationale that the Minister gave, which was incredibly ignorant of the real situation people are facing.
I think the Hon. Member heard my question earlier so I will sit down.
April 21, 1989

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her question. It is quite correct for her to assume from what I said that in fact I see what is happening here as part of a larger Tory agenda. We hear all kinds of fine language in the House about the Government's concern, commitment and so on, in this case to the future educational needs of Indian people and the Indian community. In fact, the reality on Indian reserves is dramatically different. When we look at the budgetary process that is going on here now, short months ago the Government promised all types of money to projects such as Hibernia and Fort McMurray. There was money to burn. Just a few short months later there is no money at all. We are being told to brace ourselves for next Thursday when the Budget comes down. This is why I think Canadians are responding to the issues raised in this debate. They are wondering: "Are we next?"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
