subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are probably wondering what a Member of Parliament from a Toronto riding such as Parkdale-High Park knows about this debate on post-secondary funding for natives. First, let me establish my credibility about why I want to participate in the debate.
I had the good fortune of being bom and raised in the Province of Saskatchewan where my parents started on a homestead. They farmed there for 25 years. As a young boy going to school I grew up with Indian children and their families. We did similar things to what the First Peoples did. In order to supplement our farm incomes we had to trap. As a young lad we trapped weasels to get $4 or $5 a pelt. That was good money in those days. We would snare jack-rabbits, skin them and sell the pelts.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Don't tell the NDP that.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
The Hon. Member from Brampton does not even want to listen. He is an urban boy who cannot relate to this type of pioneer life. There are probably not too many Members in the House who can, which is why I am sharing this with all Members of this House. I am sharing it to establish my credibility.
What did we do for dessert? We picked Saskatoon berries and so on with the Indians.
Supply
We took that life-style away from our first Canadians. What did we replace it with? Since we took it away from these people I think the best replacement, the best investment, is a post-secondary education.
Not all the children in my family could go on with their educations. My oldest brother had to work on the farm. He could not go on to post-secondary education. I am pleased that my parents and my country allowed me the opportunity to complete my post-secondary education at the masters and other levels. That education allowed me to go in to teaching with the Toronto Board of Education where I spent over 30 years. Most of those 30 years were spent working with exceptional students, the physically handicapped, the emotionally disturbed, the mentally handicapped, and with students who had learning disabilities, a new group that has been discovered in this category of exceptional students.
The Toronto Board of Education is a leader in North America, and probably in the world, as far as opening up new opportunities for students with all these different handicaps is concerned. People with mental handicaps never went on to post-secondary education.
Today I am very pleased that community colleges are accepting them. Students with learning disabilities are now going to universities. Many of them are very bright but have some learning disabilities, and experts to this day do not know the cause of them.
I would like to compliment universities such as York University, the University of Toronto and others that have set up special departments to accept these students into post-secondary education. Ten years ago these students would never have found themselves in a university setting. Today they have the same opportunity as many other students. At a time when universities are opening their doors to students of all abilities, of all handicaps, the Government is closing doors to the children who have the first right to attend post-secondary education.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
I could not agree more with the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) when he said a native child today has a better chance of ending up in jail than receiving a university education. This is a sad commentary for the Government and for this country.

April 21, 1989
Supply
I wanted to participate in this debate because of the students who went on the hunger strike. Is it not sad that it took a hunger strike to bring this debate to this House today? I was involved in a hunger strike five years ago. Three people in Etobicoke-Lakeshore went on a hunger strike. They had come to Canada as refugees. Their spouse and the children were caught in Poland; Poland would not allow them to join their families here. We went on a hunger strike. I saw the physical and emotional damage that was done to these hunger strikers.
I felt for the Indian students while they were striking. I would not recommend to these students to continue such tactics because if your health goes, and heaven forbid even if your life goes, you will be no good to this countiy. We need your talents. We need your expertise.
I had a hand in ending that other strike. I was the liaison person between the people on strike, our External Affairs Department and the Polish Embassy in Ottawa. I had to take messages back and forth. I was pleased when the strike finally ended.
Today I am pleased to announce, Mr. Speaker, that within a year after the hunger strikers agreed to end their strike all three families were reunited, and we have three additional happy families living here in Canada.
Let us hope that this incident ends the same way, that it ends in happiness and ends with greater opportunities for our First People at the post-secondary level.
Once again we see an example of the lack of commitment of the Government to the people in our country who are most in need of our help, our support and our generosity.
In 1984, a national review was undertaken on the First Nations educational systems. This review included recommendations from aboriginal and non-aboriginal peoples. A lot of time and energy was spent on this review, and it was forwarded to the Department of Indian Affairs in December 1988. It was in good faith that the First Nations did not expect the Government to implement any changes to the education system until there had been bilateral consultations based on the review which would subsequently lead to action that was palatable to all parties involved.
This did not happen. The Government has not responded to the review. In fact, it has once again chosen to renege on its promises. It is becoming painfully obvious that this is not an election year and because this is not an election year, the people in this country who are most in need are paying for it.
On March 20 of this year, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) decided that it was time to stop playing nice guy. He announced changes to the guidelines for First Nations' post-secondary education. He announced these changes, not in consultation with the people who would be affected by them but in consultation with his departmental officials in Ottawa. There is nothing wrong with consulting with departmental officials. I pay a high tribute to the people working in our Public Service in all Departments, but surely the Minister could have consulted with the users of the program.
These changes come at a time, in the National Chief's word, "when the First Nations are looking to the future and are planning a long-range holistic approach to education, a time when the First Nations are striving for self-government and self-reliance".
What is happening today is a travesty. If the Government is cutting back in the area of post-secondary education, what is going to happen to the other levels of education? We already know that at present there are
85,000	students utilizing educational facilities. At a minimum we would expect over 3,000 classrooms to house all these students. That is not the case. There are presently only 2,000 classrooms.
In 1977 there were 3,500 students eligible for post-secondary educational programs. Today, as we heard from the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), they number around 15,000. The numbers are increasing. The funding is being cut back. With all due respect to the Hon. Minister, the funding over the years has not taken inflation into account. Therefore any comparison is not being done in real dollars. The 10 per cent he talks about does not cover increases in educational costs, inflation increases, et cetera.
In 1987, the Government brought in new guidelines. At the same time, they introduced a cap on the budget. They promised at that time that were they to bring in more changes they would be brought in, in consultation with the First Nations. This is not what they did. They unilaterally imposed new guidelines. They unilaterally implemented changes to a program which they obviously did not understand.
April 21, 1989

Ever since the election all we have heard about is cut-backs-cut-backs in our unemployment insurance programs, cut-backs in programs that affect those who need them the most. This type of behaviour is not going to win them any votes. In fact, this behaviour has already cost them a few points in the polls. It will be very interesting to see where this Government which makes its decisions based on public opinion polls will end up in those same polls after next Thursday when the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) goes to work on the rest of the people of this country with a hack-saw.
We all know and accept that post-secondary education is an investment in the future. We have heard this from our previous debaters. This Government continues to talk about its commitment to the First Nations of this country. It continues to talk about its support for Indian self-determination, for Indian self-reliance.
I have been an educator for many years. However, it does not take an educator to know that there is an undeniable link between education, especially post-secondary education, and better employment opportunities. It boggles the mind to see what this Government is doing. It is inconceivable to me, and obviously to my colleagues here, that the route to the well-being of the First Nations is being nipped in the bud.
I will not repeat, Mr. Speaker, what the Members for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, Kenora-Rainy River, Oshawa and others have shared with this House about the difference in mortality rates, welfare rates, alcoholism, and suicide rates between the people of the First Nations and the rest of Canadians. I urge the Government to rethink its policy on post-secondary education. I urge the Government to give the First Nations a chance to prove that they are capable and competent; that they contribute to this country as much as you or I do, Mr. Speaker; that they are not a burden on society; and that they are the First Nations.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments. I want to bring it to the attention of the Hon. Member and the House that while we are concerned about funding of post-secondary education for native children because it is crucial for the equality of opportunity for native people in Canada, we must also be concerned about young native people who never make it through high school.
I am dealing with a particular case in my riding of which I believe the House should be aware. I hope Hon. Members opposite will bring it to the attention of the Government. It is the case of a young 12-year old status Indian boy who is suffering from foetal alcohol syndrome with an attention deficit disorder. This is causing severe emotional and behavioural problems. This boy was adopted at the age of one by a family living in my riding.
They are having extreme difficulty and are meeting nothing but road blocks with the federal and provincial Governments in trying to get the help this boy needs before he reaches an age where he cannot be helped, which is within the next two or three years.
The parents are at their wits' end. This young boy may never have a chance even to grow up properly, let alone go to university, with the limited funding that is available.
They have been told that the cost of the residential treatment recommended by professional advisers is $50,000 a year. That is more than the total income of the family, which is needed to provide for them and their other two adolescent children.

April 21, 1989
Supply
This morning, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Nault) spoke about the devastating cost in dollars and human potential of not providing what is needed. The funding to provide adequate treatment for this child is not available under health funding. Funding is not available because he is a status Indian. This young life will go down the drain. The cost of providing treatment for him, to give him a chance at the opportunities we are discussing today, is less than the cost of one year in prison, less than the cost of 30 days in a hospital.
The parents have approached the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In September 1988, they were told that there is no help for their son. They approached the Department of National Health and Welfare and were told there is no help for their son. They cannot turn him over to the Children's Aid Society because he is a status Indian and the band would have to be consulted on his care.
I ask Hon. Members to bring this problem to the attention of the Cabinet and to save this one young life and many others like him who will never have the opportunities we want for all our native peoples.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION FUNDING-NATIVE PEOPLES
speechtext:
I am glad my colleague has raised this point. There are thousands of cases such as this one. Because we do not have early identification, the students are spotted too late to bring them help.
I think any system of education that is funded by the federal Government should provide the same opportunities as any child gets from Kindergarten to Grade 13.

Member is saying about the situation we are now facing is blowing in the wind. It is making politics out of a very serious situation.
The Hon. Member must answer that question and state emphatically one way or the other where his Party stands on this issue. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to contribute to the debate on the topic before us today. As a preface to my comments, I would like to compliment members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition for picking this topic and for devoting two opposition days to its discussion.
In his comments this morning, the Minister said that this was a topic plagued by misunderstanding. Hopefully, through our discussions today and the subsequent ones on Monday, we can help to educate the people in the House and in the country a bit better, and this topic will be a bit better understood by everyone.
I am very concerned about the perception that some Hon. Members opposite are trying to establish, either by rhetoric or in some cases by volume, that they are the only ones who are concerned about aboriginal post-secondary education. We on this side of the House are every bit as committed to improving the economic situation of aboriginal peoples as anyone on the opposite side. However, we recognize that we have another responsibility, a responsibility to ensure that the moneys we spend on behalf of all Canadians are spent as effectively as possible.
This morning, the Minister also reflected on a view that is well shared by his colleagues on this side of the House. He said that we are as proud of this program as are the Indians of their graduates. I think that is a very profound statement and it does reflect our feelings.
The funding level of this program has increased significantly under this Government. This has resulted in significant progress on behalf of the Indian and Inuit people. The Government, through the Minister, has reinforced its commitment to the program and to supporting reasonable levels of funding based on consultation and negotiations with representatives of the native community.
It is not enough to say simply that because a program is good it should have open-ended funding. This program is a good program. It should be continued. The program is a fair and a generous one because the Government believes in the importance of the post-secondary needs of Indian students, and we are prepared to support them.

April 21, 1989
Supply
I would like to take a moment to put the current funding levels for native post-secondary student assistance into perspective. In terms of financial support to Indian students, this program is one of the most generous in the entire world. The student assistance program in Canada provides a significantly greater level of support than similar programs in other countries.
Let us compare it to the United States. Last year, the federal Government post-secondary grants to American Indians totalled $32.9 million. That supported 15,000 students. This represented 25 per cent of the funding that is provided in Canada to support for an equal number of students.
Our new policy is generous. It is fair and it can be administered by Indian authorities. It can be administered by Indian authorities in ways which best meet the needs of their students.
The Government assists Indian and Inuit students this generously because it believes in making an investment in Canada's future. Educated people prosper. Economic development opportunities open up and welfare rolls decrease.
Assistance for post-secondary education is one of the most successful programs the federal Government has ever undertaken. Since the introduction of the previous policy, the E-12 guidelines, the numbers of post-secondary students has increased from around 3,500 in 1977-78 to some 15,000 in 1988-89. In the same period, the budget for the program has grown from $9 million to close to $130 million.
The policy has been successful. Every member of the House appears to recognize its value. Nevertheless, we recognize that even the most successful policies must be updated and revised to meet changing needs and emerging trends. In the case of post-secondary education, there was a clear requirement to produce more graduates to ensure that there would be more Indian students who entered colleges and universities to complete their studies and then help make self-government and economic independence a reality for all Indian peoples. The objective of this policy is to help Indians gain access to a post-secondary education so they can pursue individual careers and contribute to the achievement of Indian self-government and economic self-reliance.
I would like now to take a couple of minutes to explain some of the benefits available to eligible students. To begin with, complete tuition assistance is provided to eligible full-time and part-time students. This category of benefits includes student fees for registration, tuition, and the cost of books and supplies required for a particular course of study. A simple example is that if a student in nursing requires a stethoscope, it is an eligible expense and it would be covered.
Full-time students who are required to live away from their permanent places of residence may receive a wide range of benefits. For example, they may qualify for a travel grant back to their homes once every semester for themselves and for any dependant who lives with them. These students will also be eligible to receive allowances to help cover their living expenses including food, rent, heat and electricity. In areas where rental costs are higher than normal, Indian students may receive a special rent supplement.
Let me cite some examples of the level of assistance. Beginning the next academic year, a single student may receive a maximum monthly living allowance of $675. A married student with an employed spouse and three dependants may receive a maximum of $1,205 per month. A single parent with three dependants will receive a maximum of $1,355 per month, plus a rental supplement where applicable.
Students will be eligible to receive funding at three levels. To complete community college diplomas or certificates, undergraduate degrees, and Masters' or professional degrees. Students allowances will be provided for the official length of the student's program, three years for a three-year program, four years for a four-year program, and so on. When required, an additional year may be provided for a student to complete a degree or diploma program at each of the three levels.
Let me put those rates into perspective. A single mother with two children in her first year of a Master's of Psychology program at the University of Regina will receive a grant of $1,205 per month to support herself and her family. Her tuition, books and supplies are paid for. She is also eligible to obtain a scholarship of up to $1,500 for the year. Expenses for travel between Regina and her normal place of residence, if it is outside Regina, will be provided once each term for her and her dependants.
April 21, 1989

A single student from a reserve in Ontario in his second year of a Bachelor of Arts Degree at the University of Ottawa would receive funding to pay his tuition, his books and supplies, and his travel from the reserve to Ottawa once each semester. In addition he is eligible to receive a grant of $675 per month from the Post-secondary Student Assistance Program to defray living expenses. If this student in his first year maintained a grade average of B-plus, he would also be eligible to receive a scholarship of $1,000 per year.
A married student with three children whose wife and children are dependent upon him for support, in his first year of studies at a Montreal CEGEP where he is hoping to complete the required courses in Business Administration, would receive a grant of $1,355 per month from the Post-secondary Student Assistance Program, above and beyond the funding he receives for tuition, books and supplies. He would also receive an allowance to enable him and his family to travel to and from his normal place of residence once every semester. If he maintains a grade average of B or better during the year, he may also be eligible to receive a scholarship of $1,000 for his next year of study.
These students may not be millionaires, but it is a significant level of support. Grants for single students living away from home are equivalent to a full-time job paying $4.96 per hour. Grants paid to single-parent students with three dependants would be equivalent to a full-time job paying $12.14 per hour.
Successful students will experience no difficulty in obtaining support to the conclusion of a professional degree like a law degree, or a graduate program such as a Master's degree or a Ph.D.
Under the terms of the new program, administering organizations such as bands, tribal councils, education authorities, or other organizations, will have an even greater opportunity to directly participate in the post-secondary education process. The new policy is sufficiently flexible to allow administering organizations to establish their own operating procedures, provided these are consistent with the policy and reflect the maximum rates and limits of assistance.
Supply
The Post-secondary Student Assistance Program is designed to encourage improvements in the level of academic achievement, resulting in a generation of Indians and Inuit who are better equipped to face the future.
I would like to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. colleagues, that the only "cap" Indian students will see in this program is a mortar-board.

I appreciate the comments made by my hon. friend. He certainly brought forward to the House an impressive list of figures and benefits that are available to Indian students. I am sure he brought those forward sincerely and respectfully. However, I do think that he misses the point of the entire debate. The major point of today's debate has to do with capping the educational opportunities of native students. We are not saying that it is not a budgetary matter or not a money matter. We have conceded or gone along with the point of view of the Government that there has been an increase in funding. We believe our point, which is sustainable and unassailable, is that there is a capping element which will ultimately limit the educational opportunities of native students. We do not think that that is a good policy, particularly for native students. However, it is not a good policy for the native community, and ultimately it is not a good policy for the country.
It has been demonstrated that the native population is under-represented in almost all major areas of the economy. I believe that all Members would like to see more native accountants, lawyers, engineers, and architects. We would like to see natives better represented in the professions, and throughout the economy. We find the unemployment figures that natives face every day loathsome, horrendous, and appalling. They face despair and desperation in their home communities on the reserves. One way to break out of that and to give them hope and the opportunity to produce and give their all to the country is through education. On this side of the House we feel that we cannot afford to miss this opportunity. We cannot afford not to give native children this opportunity.
Does the Hon. Member not understand how this policy will backfire? Ultimately it will not only harm the native students, but it will harm the country. We want to get natives off the welfare rolls and make them productive. We believe that there is a great risk that the Government's policy will backfire.

From the comments that have been shared by myself and other Members, the Minister will have support in that fight for extra money, if we have the proof that the students are there who actually need it.
The Minister involved is one of the first cabinet Ministers I met after I received my nomination last year. My riding of Red Deer in central Alberta has very few Francophones. There are a large number of students enrolled in French immersion. That is the only way to learn French, because there are not enough people who speak French on the street. Red Deer is not exactly a hotbed of labour activity. Yet in his capacity as Minister of Labour, a French-Canadian cabinet Minister came to Red Deer to present a cheque and a grant to the Canadian Labour Congress and to meet the press. A man who is willing to do that will not be afraid to negotiate with people and meet them anywhere. I am convinced that this Minister's door is open, that he is honest and sincere and willing to meet people and discuss issues with them. There have been numerous discussions with native groups throughout the past year. He has already changed the original policy based on those negotiations.
Personally, I am convinced if the need is proved he will change it again. I do not think that it is a good policy for government to spend money open-ended on any program regardless of how good it is. We cannot write a blank cheque. We have to know where the money is going.

Every one of us here has heard discussions today that if we do not expand this program and leave it open-ended, we are encouraging a continuation of the unfortunate situation that exists in all too many Indian reservations today, a situation of welfare payments and substandard living standards.
